questions.text: Explain the difference between Terraform state and your Git repository
questions.answer: Git holds the *declared intent*: the configuration, its history, who changed it and why. State holds the *observed reality*: for each declared resource, the provider's actual ID, its current attributes, and the dependencies Terraform resolved when it created it. They are different kinds of data with different lifecycles. Git is append-only and reviewed; state is a mutable binary-ish blob that changes on every apply, is locked during operations, and — critically — contains sensitive attributes in plaintext. The consequence people miss: because state is the only mapping from a logical address like aws_instance.web to i-0abc123, losing or corrupting state does not "lose the servers" — it makes Terraform believe those servers do not exist and try to create replacements. That is why state is backed up to versioned object storage, why it is encrypted, and why deleting it is an incident, not a cleanup. I would also say what state is *not*: not a source of truth about desired state (Git is), and not a backup mechanism (it is the most recent snapshot of what exists, not a point-in-time recoverable history of your data).

questions.text: What is drift, how do you detect it, and when is drift acceptable?
questions.answer: Drift is the gap between what Terraform recorded and what the provider API reports — usually because somebody changed something in the console, or because another system legitimately owns a field. Detection is terraform plan -refresh-only, run on a schedule in CI and posted as a diff; a clean plan is the only real proof of parity. Acceptable drift is when another controller legitimately owns that attribute: an autoscaler writing desired_capacity, a managed service writing its own status fields, Kubernetes controllers writing spec fields. In that case I declare ownership explicitly with a narrowly scoped ignore_changes — one attribute, never all — and I monitor the owner instead. Unacceptable drift is anything security- or data-related: a widened security group, a public bucket, a changed encryption setting. For those, the fix is not ignore_changes; it is removing console write access (SCP/permission boundary) so drift stops being possible, plus a plan to reconcile. The distinction I make in review: ignore_changes is a declaration of ownership, and using it to silence a real problem is how a security group stays open for a year.

questions.text: Your terraform plan shows -/+ on a resource. Is that safe?
questions.answer: Not automatically. -/+ means Terraform will destroy and recreate, because some attribute is ForceNew and the provider does not offer an in-place update. That has three classes of risk: identity (a new resource ID — an ENI gets a new private IP, a DNS record points at a new target), data (if the resource holds state you cannot recreate), and availability (the resource is genuinely gone for the duration of the replacement). So my answer is: read the plan's change.actions and the attribute that forces it, then decide by class. For an RDS cluster, changing the major version or a ForceNew parameter is a replacement, and I would use a clone-and-cutover, not a replacement. For a security group, replacement means traffic in flight sees a window with no rules. For an instance with an attached ENI, replacement means DNS staleness. The correct engineering response is layered: prevent_destroy for anything stateful (so an accidental apply fails at plan time), create_before_destroy where identity must persist, tests in a state-clone environment, and a change window with a snapshot. I would never raise the Terraform timeout to make a replacement "fit"; I would redesign it.

questions.text: Explain the AWS shared responsibility model, and where is the boundary for RDS?
questions.answer: The provider is responsible for security *of* the cloud — hardware, facility, hypervisor, host OS, physical network. The customer is responsible for security *in* the cloud — data, IAM policies, network configuration, and the guest OS on EC2. The interesting part, and what I would add unprompted, is that the boundary moves with the service, and for RDS it is narrower than people assume. AWS owns the host, storage, replication, and backup infrastructure. I still own the data, the schema, grants and roles, iam_auth, TLS settings, parameter group values (including anything with pending-reboot), extension versions, and every query. A managed database gives me patching and failover; it gives me nothing about whether my parameter group is sane. And there is no shared-responsibility escape from IAM: AWS owns the implementation of the IAM service, and I own every single policy in the account. Least privilege is entirely on me.

questions.text: How do you design least-privilege IAM for a service?
questions.answer: I treat it as a loop, not a setting. First, run the workload under a permissive role for a few days and read CloudTrail to learn what it actually calls. Then write a policy that grants exactly that, plus known planned needs, scoped by resource ARN — table, not *; bucket prefix, not bucket; a specific KMS key, not kms:*. Then wrap it in a fail-closed guardrail: an SCP or permission boundary so a mistake in the identity policy cannot exceed the ceiling. Then run Access Analyzer's "unused access" analysis for 30 days and delete what was never used, and repeat monthly. Two details that matter in review: conditions are where the real power is (aws:SourceVpce, aws:PrincipalOrgID, aws:SourceArn, s3:prefix), and the classic escalation is iam:PassRole combined with a service permission — Access Analyzer's policy validation now rejects that class by default, and I make sure it is on. For humans: SSO with short-lived sessions and MFA, never access keys. For workloads: roles everywhere — instance profiles, task roles — so there is no long-lived key on a machine to leak.

questions.text: What is the difference between a stateful and a stateless resource, and why does it change your deployment strategy?
questions.answer: Stateful means the resource holds data whose loss or duplication is user-visible: databases, queues, buckets, disks. Stateless means any instance can serve any request and losing one is uninteresting: web servers, caches, API replicas. The strategy difference is the tolerance for replacement. Stateless replacement is a non-event — start a new one, drain the old, delete it. Stateful replacement is a data event, which is why you want blue/green with replication, snapshots before changes, prevent_destroy, and a tested restore. The second difference is which side of the rollout can be rolled back. Stateless deploys roll forward/backward by swapping which instances are live. Stateful deploys roll forward by *contract-then-expand*: add a nullable column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, drop the old. Destructive DDL cannot be rolled back, so it cannot be in the same deploy as the code that stops using the old column. The third, which people forget: statefulness determines your scale-down policy. A stateless tier can scale to zero or one; a stateful tier needs warm capacity because restoring or re-replicating from cold takes minutes during an incident.

questions.text: Walk me through an Nginx request lifecycle
questions.answer: A worker process accepts the connection, parses the request, matches server by SNI/Host and location by prefix/regex/exact, performs the TLS handshake if it is an ssl server, evaluates limit_req/limit_conn, selects an upstream server by the pool's algorithm, opens a connection to it (proxy_connect_timeout), sends the request with rewritten headers (proxy_http_version 1.1, Host, X-Forwarded-*), reads the response (proxy_read_timeout between reads, proxy_send_timeout for the request body), optionally buffers it to memory or disk, writes it to the client with add_headers applied, and logs with the timings. Two things I always mention because they are the most common bugs: proxy_pass with a trailing slash rewrites the URI, and proxy_set_header Connection "" is required (with keepalive in the upstream) or you get no connection reuse at all. And the concurrency arithmetic: worker_processes × worker_connections / 2 is the maximum concurrent proxied requests, because each one consumes a client socket and an upstream socket, and the LimitNOFILE in the systemd unit must match.

questions.text: You added a rate limit and throughput dropped. Why?
questions.answer: In order of likelihood: (1) I used delay instead of nodelay, so bursts are smoothed at the configured rate and every client pays up to burst/rate seconds of latency; (2) the zone is too small, so keys are evicted and the module's state churns — the error log says "could not allocate node in the shared zone", and eviction effectively *allows* traffic while doing it; (3) the key is $binary_remote_addr behind a CDN, so either everyone shares one bucket or, if I keyed on X-Forwarded-For without set_real_ip_from restricting who may set it, a client can rotate their header to bypass the limit entirely; (4) limit_req_status is still the default 503, so dashboards attribute throttling to the backend and someone "fixes" the backend. I would also note the cost angle: SQS-style request pricing makes polling the bill, so rate limiting interacts with your observability bill too.

questions.text: Explain HSTS and when preload is a bad idea
questions.answer: HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security) tells the browser to refuse plaintext HTTP to this host for max-age seconds. The risk is that it is a one-way door: once a browser has cached it, you cannot recall it from the client, and any legitimate plaintext HTTP to that host — a health-check poller on an http subdomain, an internal redirect, a legacy integration — fails until the header changes *and* the browser cache expires. includeSubDomains extends it to every subdomain, so one misconfigured internal host breaks everything beneath it. preload is stricter still: browsers require it to be at least a year, and submitting the domain to the preload list means users who have never visited it are also locked in. So the practice is to stage it: max-age=300, watch, then max-age=86400, then a year — and add includeSubDomains only after an inventory shows every subdomain is HTTPS-only. And in Nginx, use add_header ... always;, or the header disappears on exactly the error responses where you least want to lose it.

questions.text: Why did my service 502 on every deploy, and why did staging not show it?
questions.answer: The 502s are a drain problem: the load balancer removed the target (or sent SIGTERM) while in-flight requests were still running. The three timeouts that must be ordered are deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds ≥ the longest request, stopTimeout/terminationGracePeriodSeconds ≥ the drain time, and a preStop sleep so the endpoint controller learns the pod is going away before the process stops accepting. Staging missed it because of a *ratio*, not a difference in kind. Staging had near-zero traffic, so almost nothing was in flight when the pod stopped, so the window between "target removed" and "process exits" contained no requests. Production had a p99 of 20 seconds, so that window always contained requests. That is a genuine parity gap and it argues for testing deploy behaviour under load in staging — a load test that exercises a deploy — rather than assuming green staging means safe deploys.

questions.text: Terraform, Ansible, or both? Where is the line?
questions.answer: Different abstraction levels, so use both. Terraform owns things that exist in a cloud API and have identity: VPCs, subnets, instances, RDS, IAM, DNS, queues. Ansible owns the *inside* of a machine: users, packages, systemd units, config files, log rotation, an agent installed on a host Terraform did not create. The distinguishing concept is idempotence. Terraform is a reconciler with a graph and a plan, so re-running is free. Ansible is imperative; it is only safe to re-run if each action is idempotent — declarative modules that report changed=0 on the second run. That is why shell: echo ... >> is bad and template:/apt: state=present is good, and why --check --diff is a meaningful dry run. The overlap zone is where it goes wrong: if Terraform writes a systemd unit via user_data and Ansible also writes it, the last writer wins silently. My rule: each fact has exactly one owner, and ownership is documented.

questions.text: Your IaC state is on an S3 bucket. What are the security requirements, and why?
questions.answer: Five things. Encryption at rest with a customer-managed KMS key, and bucket policy assertions denying unencrypted puts, so the default cannot be bypassed.

questions.text: How do you safely roll out infrastructure changes?
questions.answer: Static analysis and validation first, then a plan artifact from a read-only role, then a policy gate, then approval, then apply *that same artifact* from CI. Applying the stored plan is the important detail: terraform apply -auto-approve re-plans, so what you reviewed is not necessarily what ran. Blast-radius control is layered: state split per domain and per blast radius, so a bad route table cannot touch the cluster; prevent_destroy on anything stateful; create_before_destroy where identity must persist; approval gates on destroy, IAM, security groups, KMS and anything reducing redundancy; canary accounts first; and change windows for the destructive ones. Rollback is not "revert": state is not a deployment. The default is forward-fix — revert the commit and apply — which works for every non-destructive change. State revert works when the code is right and the *run* went wrong halfway. Restore-from-backup is the only option for destructive changes, which is the whole argument for versioning, PITR, and prevent_destroy.

questions.text: Explain the difference between IaaS, PaaS, and serverless, with the real trade-offs
questions.answer: They differ in how much of the stack the provider operates. IaaS: I own the OS and everything above. PaaS: I own the app and the data. Serverless: I own the code and the provider owns the instance lifecycle — the servers are still there, I just cannot see them, which is the honest framing. The three properties that make serverless what it is: no servers to provision, pay-per-use, and elastic scale-out *and* down. Everything else is a consequence: execution limits (15 minutes for Lambda), cold starts, no long-lived sockets, and a much harder debugging story because you do not have a host to inspect. The trade-off I would state explicitly: serverless wins on idle cost and operational effort, and loses on control, execution duration, and latency predictability. So for a spiky, event-driven, request-shaped workload with generous latency tolerance I would use it; for a steady, low-latency, protocol-heavy service I would use managed containers or instances. And the middle ground people miss is "managed containers" (ECS/Fargate, Cloud Run, Container Apps), which gets scale-to-zero *and* long-running processes and custom networking, and is often the right answer.

questions.text: What is a Region, what is an AZ, and why are AZ letters unreliable?
questions.answer: A Region is an independent, geographically separate deployment of the cloud — its own control plane, its own quotas. An AZ is one or more discrete data centres inside a Region with independent power, cooling, and networking. Regions are chosen for latency, compliance, and service availability; AZs are chosen for failure tolerance. AZ letters are not a stable identity: AWS does not publish which physical data centre each letter maps to, and that mapping can differ between accounts and change over time. So us-east-1a in my account is not necessarily the same building as us-east-1a in yours, and I must never hardcode letters — I discover the AZs from the account's own availability-zones API, and where I need true identity (EBS volume co-location, legal constraints) I map to AZ IDs like use1-az2. Two more details worth stating: AZ counts differ per region (most have three; some have six), and cross-AZ traffic is both charged and adds latency, so spreading across AZs has a real cost that people forget when they plan the bill.

questions.text: How do you design a VPC for a three-tier application?
questions.answer: Six AZs of thinking, then the concrete shape. Public subnets in three AZs for the ALB only. Private app subnets in three AZs, each with its own NAT gateway for zonal high availability — one NAT for all subnets makes every AZ depend on one AZ, and that is a real outage class I have seen. Isolated subnets for RDS, with no route to the internet. Security groups referencing each other rather than CIDRs (so the rules follow the SGs), and egress that is explicitly allowed only where needed, because SG egress is deny-by-default and someone always forgets that. Then the parts people miss: CIDR planning with room to grow (/20 per subnet from a /16, not /24, because IP exhaustion is an outage in Kubernetes); a route to an S3 gateway endpoint in every private route table so S3 and DynamoDB traffic does not go out through NAT (this is both a cost and an availability win); flow logs on REJECT; and validation — you cannot declare multi-AZ resilience without having failed over and watched it. I would end with: the routing table is the security boundary as much as the SG, and the longest-prefix-match rule is why "there are two routes to 0.0.0.0/0" is not a conflict you get to ignore.

questions.text: What are burstable instances, and when are they the wrong choice?
questions.answer: T-family instances have a *baseline* of about 20% of their vCPUs, and they accumulate credits when you use less than the baseline and spend them when you use more, up to full capacity. When credits run out, the hypervisor throttles the instance to baseline — performance drops abruptly and the CPU metric still looks high. So they are wrong for anything with steady load above ~20% of the allocated vCPUs, which in practice means most real services: a service idling at 5% and spiking to 80% for short periods is the ideal Burstable workload; a service consistently at 45% will accumulate a debt and be throttled on a schedule you cannot predict, which shows up as unexplained p99 latency. Practically: alarm on CPUSurplusCreditBalance, use m/c families for steady services, and remember that t4g is Graviton (cheaper, ARM images required) while t3 is Intel.

questions.text: Compare S3 storage classes and give me a decision rule
questions.answer: The axes are retrieval time, minimum storage duration, and minimum object size. Standard is milliseconds and no commitments. Standard-IA is milliseconds but bills 128 KiB minimum per object and requires 30 days. One Zone-IA is cheaper but an AZ loss is data loss. Glacier Instant is milliseconds; Flexible is minutes to hours with a 90-day minimum; Deep Archive is 5–12 hours with a 180-day minimum. The decision rule I use: how long can you wait to read it, and how often do you read it? If you cannot state a maximum acceptable read latency, you do not belong in Glacier. And never use a lower durability class for the only copy. The traps I would mention unprompted: the IA minimum object size (a 4 KiB object bills as 128 KiB), early-deletion charges (deleting a Flexible object at day 40 costs you through day 90), and unfinished multipart uploads costing money invisibly — so the lifecycle rule with AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload is mandatory, not optional.

questions.text: Is S3 strongly consistent? What is not guaranteed?
questions.answer: Yes for the current version of objects: since December 2020 S3 is strongly read-after-write consistent for GET, PUT, DELETE, LIST, and HEAD, including overwrites and delete markers. What is *not* guaranteed is more interesting and is what I would say next: consistency between concurrent writers to the same key (last-write-wins, no ordering, no merge); consistency of anything *derived* from S3 — a search index, a CDN cache, a metadata table, a data-lake sync; the propagation of IAM policy changes (up to minutes); and the delivery of S3 event notifications, which is at-least-once and can be duplicated. So the accurate statement to a colleague is: "S3 is consistent, my *system* is eventually consistent, and my consumers must be idempotent."

questions.text: When and how do you use presigned URLs?
questions.answer: To let a client upload or download directly, without proxying bytes through my API servers, and without giving the client AWS credentials. The URL carries a signature over a specific action and key, and its lifetime is bounded by the credential's session, so I generate it per request rather than caching it. The security requirements I would insist on: the key is generated server-side with a per-user prefix (uploads/{userId}/{uuid}) so one user's signing cannot write another user's path; the signature is for one key and one action, never a prefix; I enforce Content-Type and a size range with bucket policy conditions so a client cannot upload an HTML file that later gets served as a page from my origin; and presigned URLs are treated as bearer credentials everywhere, which means never logging them — query strings need redaction in the log pipeline, and they should be in your secret-scanning config. For very large files, multipart upload with CreateMultipartUpload plus UploadPart; for the lifecycle side, a rule that aborts incomplete uploads after 7 days.

questions.text: How does the Lambda execution model work, and what are the real limits?
questions.answer: An invocation is either synchronous (the caller waits) or asynchronous (retries twice with backoff, then DLQ). Each execution environment handles one request at a time, so concurrency equals the number of environments — which is the key mental model for cold starts. The INIT phase (module load, imports, module-level clients) runs once per environment; the Invoke phase runs per request. That asymmetry is the whole cold start discussion. The limits I would quote: 15-minute maximum timeout, 128 MB–10 GB memory, 512 MB /tmp, 6 MB sync payload, ~1,000 unreserved concurrency per region per account, reserved concurrency as a hard cap, and account-wide ceilings on some resources. Two of those are operational landmines: reserved concurrency is both a floor and a cap (reserving 1,000 on one function means every other function has zero unreserved and throttles *instantly*), and exceeding throttles looks exactly like "the database is slow". And the economics: the bill is requests × GB-seconds, with memory as a multiplier. So batching ten records per invocation instead of ten invocations is usually a 5–10× saving with better cold-start economics, and a function whose average duration is above a second is usually mis-shaped.

questions.text: Your Lambda scale to 200 and the database fell over. Explain and fix
questions.answer: That is almost always connection exhaustion, not a database failure: 200 concurrent Lambda environments each open a pool, max_connections is reached, Postgres starts rejecting, and the appearance is a database outage. The fixes, in order of preference: RDS Proxy (or PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode) so connections are multiplexed rather than multiplied; setting max_connections from memory (work_mem × expected concurrent queries × 2) rather than accepting the class default; and if the workload is genuinely spiky, Aurora Serverless v2 which scales ACUs rather than connections. There is a second-order problem they usually want you to name: failover plus retries means duplicate writes unless writes are idempotent. After a DB failover the app reconnects and retries, and if the write is not protected by an idempotency key you get duplicate charges or duplicate orders — which is precisely the failure in the postmortem in Problem 9. So: proxy or pooler, sane max_connections, and idempotent writes with jittered retry.

questions.text: Explain SQS visibility timeout, DLQ, and batching — and how they interact
questions.answer: Visibility timeout is how long a message is hidden from other consumers after being received. If a consumer takes longer than the timeout to finish, another consumer gets the same message and processes it concurrently — the classic duplicate. The rule is that visibility timeout must exceed the worst-case processing time by a healthy margin, and in practice the SRE Workbook suggests ~6× the function timeout, or you renew the visibility timeout while working. DLQ: a redrive policy moves a message to a dead-letter queue after maxReceiveCount. That is your poison-message circuit breaker. Without it, one bad message retries forever and blocks throughput while hiding a real bug. Batching is the biggest cost lever, because SQS bills per *request*: receiving ten messages in one call costs a tenth of ten calls. And then you need partial-batch failure — ReportBatchItemFailures — so one bad message does not fail the whole batch. And the property people forget: SQS is at-least-once. Batching and visibility do not change that. Idempotent consumers are mandatory, which I implement with a uniqueness constraint on the message id and a conditional insert, so the second delivery is a no-op that returns success.

questions.text: What guarantees does "exactly once" actually give you?
questions.answer: Almost none, end to end. What exists: at-least-once delivery from SQS, SNS, EventBridge, and S3 notifications, with the possibility of duplicates and out-of-order messages. Exactly-once processing for SQS FIFO *within* the five-minute deduplication window, plus strict ordering per message group. Exactly-once delivery for Kafka within a partition if you use transactions plus read-committed consumers. Nothing gives you exactly-once *effects* on an external system you do not control. So the engineering answer is: guarantee idempotent effects. Concretely, I write the message id to a table with a unique constraint as part of the same transaction as the business change — the transactional outbox / inbox pattern — so either both happen or neither. Then duplicates are harmless, ordering is handled explicitly, and the system is resilient to any number of redeliveries. The follow-up they like: "what is the cost?" — an extra index and insert per message, and you must garbage-collect the inbox table. That is the correct trade.

questions.text: "The API is down" — how do you find the failing component?
questions.answer: "Down" is not a useful starting hypothesis; I translate it into: which user journey, which percentage, which regions, since when, and what changed. Then I look at three layers in order: my SLI (availability ratio and latency for that journey), then the dependency panel, then the deploy markers. The disciplined move is to mitigate before diagnosing: roll back the last change, kill a feature flag, scale up, or fail over — whichever is available — while a second person writes the timeline. Diagnosing under customer impact wastes the cheapest resource you have, which is time. The specific failure I would narrate is the circuit-breaker case: a timeout-and-retry change multiplied the failure count past the dependency's breaker threshold; the breaker is per-process state, so scaling out made it worse by adding more failing instances; and the only effective mitigation was rollback plus waiting out the cooldown. The lesson generalises: when a mitigation has no effect, that is information — it means the cause is not where you were looking, and you should say so out loud and change hypothesis rather than trying mitigation variant B.

questions.text: When do you use CloudFront, and what are the traps?
questions.answer: CloudFront when you want global latency, origin offload, DDoS absorption, and edge auth/WAF — most often for static assets from S3 and for whole-site caching in front of an ALB. The traps, in order of severity. Caching authenticated responses: if the cache key does not vary on Authorization (or you do not pass a custom cache policy), one user's data is served to another — that is a critical security bug and it is common. The custom-error 404→200 SPA fallback applied distribution-wide, which turns every API 404 into a 200 and poisons your error rate and your SLO. Query strings: by default CloudFront does not forward or key on them, so ?id= variants serve each other. Origin IP allowlists breaking, because the origin now sees CloudFront's IPs — publish and automate that list. Certificates in the wrong region: CloudFront needs us-east-1; API Gateway regional needs the API's region. And the operational practice I would insist on: content-hashed asset paths and no invalidation, rather than path/* invalidation on every deploy.

questions.text: Explain the AWS/GCP/Azure mapping and where it breaks
questions.answer: The names map cleanly for the primitives: EC2 ↔ Compute Engine ↔ VMs, S3 ↔ Cloud Storage ↔ Blob, ECS/EKS ↔ GKE ↔ AKS, Lambda ↔ Cloud Functions/Cloud Run ↔ Functions/Container Apps, ELB+CloudFront ↔ global external ALB ↔ Front Door, SNS/SQS ↔ Pub/Sub ↔ Service Bus/Event Grid. It breaks in four places, and these are what I would volunteer. Identity: Azure's Entra ID is a whole IAM platform with RBAC layered on, while AWS and GCP keep IAM simple and bolt federation on — so designs start from different places. Global load balancing and routing features differ in syntax and in what health data they use. Managed Postgres differs semantically: Aurora's clone-and-fast-delete, AlloyDB's columnar storage, and Azure's Flexible Server defaults mean the same migration behaves differently in promotion. And scaling models for serverless containers: ECS scales on ALB request-per-target, Cloud Run on CPU/memory/concurrency requests, Container Apps on KEDA scalers. Same idea, three models. Terraform is the only IaC that genuinely spans all three — but it standardises the *workflow*, not the semantics: eventual consistency, IAM propagation, and availability behaviour all remain provider-specific.

questions.text: Explain serverless cold starts and how you reduce them honestly
questions.answer: Decompose the latency: platform queueing, sandbox creation (40–150ms, runtime dependent), runtime init, *your* init (imports, module-level clients, config, TLS handshakes — often the biggest and most controllable term), then handler work. Only the init phase is cold; everything after the first invocation in that environment is warm. So if your handler is 5ms and your imports take 300ms, cold p99 is roughly 60× warm p99 — that asymmetry is the whole story. The reduction ladder, in order of real payoff: make INIT cheap (bundle to one file, tree-shake, lazy-load, defer heavy requires); reduce per-invocation work and reuse clients; pick a fast-starting runtime and enough memory (memory scales CPU); then architecture — do not put a cold-sensitive path on the front of a synchronous request; and only then keep-warm mechanisms. On keeping warm, honestly: Provisioned Concurrency costs roughly \$0.36/day per 1 GB environment, so ~\$11/month per environment, and you pay it at zero traffic. Schedule pings are cheap per invocation but generate load and are increasingly throttled or detected. SnapStart helps Java specifically. And the honest answer is that most teams discover their "cold start problem" is actually a slow endpoint — so measure cold p99 as a separate series, with an explicit flag, before spending money.

questions.text: Explain circuit breakers and when to fail open versus closed
questions.answer: A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that is failing, so the failure is fast instead of consuming your timeouts, your threads, and your connection pool. Closed → (rolling window failure rate over threshold) → Open → (reset timeout) → Half-open → (N successes) → Closed, or back to Open. Design details that matter: evaluate over a rolling window with a minimum request volume, not consecutive failures (a 50% error rate never trips a consecutive-failure breaker); scope per dependency and per instance; expose state as a metric and alert on *time spent open* rather than on transitions. Fail open or closed is a per-dependency correctness decision. Payments, auth, and writes fail closed — returning an error is better than a wrong or unauthorised result. Optional reads — recommendations, analytics, enrichment — fail open, serving stale or cached data, because availability beats freshness there. The subtle production issue is thundering herd on recovery: the breaker is per-process, so a fleet opens independently and then all half-opens at once. Mitigate with a shared breaker or a jittered, slow half-open.

questions.text: Why do timeouts cause cascading failures, and how do you budget them?
questions.answer: A timeout is the unit of resource holding. Without a short one, every slow request occupies a thread, a connection, and memory for as long as the dependency takes — 30 seconds by default is catastrophic at any concurrency. So threads exhaust, the pool starves, queues build, memory grows, GC pauses lengthen, and the service degrades in a way that has nothing to do with the original dependency. That is why missing timeouts are the single most reliable cause of cascading failure. The budgeting discipline: every network call gets a deadline, each hop's deadline is smaller than its caller's remaining budget, and the total along the path — *including retries and backoff* — must be less than the end-to-end SLO and less than the load balancer's idle timeout. In practice: connect timeout an order of magnitude smaller than read timeout; propagate the deadline so downstream cannot exceed it; and enforce the arithmetic with a unit test, because it is exactly the kind of invariant that silently breaks when someone adds a retry.

questions.text: What are the three pillars, and which one would you choose if you could only keep one?
questions.answer: Metrics are aggregated numeric series — cheap, low-cardinality, aggregatable, long retention; they detect and they are what you alert on. Logs are discrete structured events — expensive, high-cardinality, the best tool for "what exactly happened to this request". Traces are the causal tree of one request across services — the only pillar that shows where time and errors accumulate across a boundary. If I could keep one: metrics, because without detection everything else is theoretical — you cannot alert, cannot compute an SLI, cannot know you have a problem. But I would immediately argue that metrics-only gives you detection without explanation, which is why a real on-call system needs at least metrics plus a way to get from a symptom to a cause. In practice that is metrics for detection, logs for the specific event, traces for the cross-service structure — and the join key that makes it work is trace_id appearing in every log line.

questions.text: How do you decide what to alert on?
questions.answer: Page only when a human must act now to protect users or the business. That means user-visible symptoms measured against an SLO, imminent irreversible events (disk full before it is full, certificate expiry inside 72 hours, a failing backup), and loss of observability itself (telemetry blackouts are incidents). Everything else — CPU, memory, queue depth, cache hit rate, drift, certificate expiry at 14 days, cost anomalies — is a dashboard panel or a ticket. The reason is measurable: cause-based paging has a probabilistic relationship to harm, so it both misses real problems and produces false wakeups; and false wakeups are what train engineers to ignore pages, which destroys the whole system. The implementation is SLO-based multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting: a short window for speed and a long window for confidence, anded together, so a momentary spike does not page but a sustained 14.4× burn does. And I audit the alert inventory quarterly with actual fire counts, deleting anything that has never led to an action.

questions.text: What is an error budget and how does it change engineering decisions?
questions.answer: The error budget is the allowed failure time: 1 − SLO over the SLO window, expressed as minutes. A 99.9% objective over 28 days allows about 40 minutes of unavailability. What matters is what you do with it: it converts "reliability versus speed" from an argument into a rule. The policy is a threshold ladder: above 50% remaining, ship normally; 25–50%, reliability work first and a reduced cadence; below 25%, a freeze on non-essential changes with a named owner and a burn-down plan; zero, a feature freeze until the SLO is restored for a full window. And it must be enforced by the pipeline with human owners for exceptions, or it is a suggestion. Two subtleties I would raise: some objectives are not burn-rate-alertable and should be hard gates instead (a correctness SLO of 100% — one wrong charge is a page, not a budget decision); and a budget spent by an external dependency still counts, because users still felt it, which is why you need a written external-dependency policy (see Problem 7 §9).

questions.text: How do you make health checks correct?
questions.answer: Three probes with three meanings, and the rule that people violate most:

questions.text: Walk me through an incident from detection to postmortem
questions.answer: Detection is usually an SLO burn-rate alert; acknowledgement within minutes via the on-call. Then: declare severity based on user impact, not technical drama, open a channel, name an incident commander who does *not* debug, a scribe, and a comms owner, and start the timeline document. Scope it in the first ten minutes: which journeys, what percentage, since when, and what changed — deploy markers first. Then mitigate, preferring rollback, then feature flag, then scale, then failover, then rate limit, then a restart (documented as a mitigation, not a fix). Verify recovery on user-visible signals held stable for 15–30 minutes, not on the error count dropping once. Communicate throughout: internal update every 15 minutes even if the update is "no change", and a status page within 15 minutes for a user-visible SEV1, in a fixed message format, never speculating about the cause in public. Then: incident resolved within 48 hours, and a blameless postmortem with quantified impact, a real timeline, systemic root causes (not human error), "what went well" and "where we got lucky", and action items that are specific, owned, dated, and *verified* — plus a 30-day review to confirm they landed.

questions.text: What makes a postmortem actually change things?
questions.answer: Three tests. Is it specific? "Improve alerting" is worthless; "add a PaymentsPspLatency SLI page at p99 > 2s, owner, due date, verify by test-firing in staging" is a change. Is it owned by a person, with a date? Teams do not own deadlines. Is it verified? There should be a column that says how we will know it worked — a test that fails against the pre-fix code, a chaos experiment re-run, a metric that must improve. Beyond the items: the root cause must be systemic. "A human made a mistake" produces action items that are all reminders, and it destroys the information flow that the next incident depends on. I want multiple contributing factors, each with the minutes it cost, because that tells you which one to fix first. And I want "what went well" and "where we got lucky" recorded, because they tell you which defences to keep and which near-misses to instrument. Finally: a 30-day review is part of the deliverable, and if the same failure mode appears twice, escalate to a design review instead of patching symptoms again.

questions.text: How do you keep on-call sustainable?
questions.answer: Measure it, then attack the measurement. On-call time above 25% of engineering capacity is a red flag; pages per engineer per week and the fraction of pages that led to a real action (alert precision) say whether the signal is worth anything. The levers: rotate with overlap and compensation and freeze risky changes during the rotation week; run follow-the-sun if you are 24×7 so nobody gets a 3am page alone; delete and retune alerts that never lead to action; measure toil (everything repetitive on a page) and automate the top three by hours per month — the known mitigations in the runbook first, with limits, an audit log, and a kill switch; and write runbooks that are one page per alert, copy-pasteable, linked from the alert annotation, and tested in game days. The failure mode to name is "no time for improvement work because we are always on call" — that is a self-reinforcing loop, and the only exit is funding reliability work with the toil numbers as the business case.

questions.text: What is chaos engineering, and when is it appropriate?
questions.answer: Disciplined, hypothesis-driven fault injection to verify that the system fails the way it is designed to. The loop: define a measurable steady-state invariant, state a falsifiable hypothesis, design with an explicit blast radius and an abort condition, run it, and treat the *disproved* hypotheses as the valuable output. Appropriate when you have SLOs, automated deploys and rollbacks, a monitoring system that can detect the invariant, and a way to limit blast radius. Not appropriate when observability is weak, deploys are manual, the blast radius cannot be limited, or you are mid-incident. My defaults: start in staging to validate the injection and the abort path, then one canary service in production, then widen; automatic stop conditions expressed in terms of the SLO (stop if error rate > 5% for 60s); every experiment documented and repeatable; and the moment an experiment finds a gap, that gap becomes an action item *and* a permanent regression test. I would also run the human versions — forget a secret, delete a config, use a stale dashboard — because most real incidents are accidental human-failure experiments.

questions.text: Describe your reliability patterns and how they interact
questions.answer: The five are retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and hedging, and the thing an interviewer is really asking is whether you understand they multiply.

questions.text: Where does the money go in a cloud bill, and what do you do first?
questions.answer: In order of typical magnitude: idle capacity (40–60% of a compute bill), data transfer and egress (10–25%), storage volume *and request* pricing, over-provisioned managed services, then logs/metrics cardinality, then licences, then small surprises (elastic IPs, unattached disks, orphan snapshots, forgotten staging). Process: tag everything so cost is attributable (owner, env, service, cost-center, enforced at deploy time); then find waste (idle resources, no-login images, incomplete multipart uploads, snapshots kept "just in case", 24/7 staging); then over-provisioning, right-sized from p95/p99 over a month, not from an average; then commitments — Savings Plans/reserved *last*, only for the measured stable baseline after rightsizing, because committing to an over-provisioned fleet wastes the saving; then storage classes with access analysis via S3 access logs before you transition; then NAT and cross-AZ traffic, which is where structural wins live (VPC endpoints); then request-priced services, where the fix is architecture (batching) rather than settings. And the most senior part is what I *do not* do: I do not cut metrics or logs below what incident response needs, I do not reduce replicas below the number that supports the SLO, I do not delete the only physical backup because PITR exists, and I do not move production to Spot. Cost optimisation that increases your incident rate is a loss.

practice.afterTopic: Reliability patterns: retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, hedging
items: Terraform and IaC
State vs Git? State is the observed reality (IDs, attributes, bindings); Git is the declared intent. State is mutable, locked, and secret-bearing.
sensitive = true? Redacts CLI output only. It does not encrypt state. Use ephemeral and Secrets Manager.
Two applies at once? Both plan from the same serial; the second write clobbers the first. Hence locking plus a prod-only CI writer role.
-target? Applies a fragment and skips the rest of the graph. Emergency repair only, then backfill the code.
count vs for_each? count reindexes when the list length changes (destroy/recreate churn); for_each keys are stable.
moved block? Refactors addresses without destroying — the safe way to rename or restructure.
prevent_destroy? Turns an accidental destroy into a failed plan. Use on anything stateful.
state rm? Forgets a resource. It does not delete it. The danger is the *next* apply recreating it.
state mv? Reassigns a resource to a new address in state, no cloud API call.
Drift detection command? terraform plan -refresh-only, scheduled in CI, reported as a diff.
Provider pinning? version = "~> 5.60.0" and commit .terraform.lock.hcl. Pin patches, widen deliberately.
Why does the plan show -/+? An attribute is ForceNew, so the API requires destroy + create. Read the actions, then judge by data/identity/availability risk.
Workspace vs environment? A workspace is a pointer to a different *state file* for the same config. It does not namespace variables, and it is not a security boundary.
When do you use -target? Only for break-glass repair, and only with a follow-up code backfill.
Module or copy-paste? Modules. Copy-paste diverges by definition; the environment supplies data, not behaviour.
Cloud: AWS
Region vs AZ? Region is an independent cloud deployment; AZ is a discrete data centre inside it with independent power and network.
Why not hardcode us-east-1a? AZ letter → data centre mapping is account-specific and can change. Discover AZs; use AZ IDs for identity.
Shared responsibility? Provider secures *of* the cloud (hardware, hypervisor, host); you secure *in* it (data, IAM, config, guest OS).
RDS boundary? Provider: host, storage, replication, backup infra. You: data, schema, grants, parameter groups, TLS, extension versions.
IAM evaluation order? Identity policies → resource policies → session policies → SCPs → boundaries. Explicit deny wins; then any allow; else implicit deny.
Privilege escalation to watch? iam:PassRole + a service permission. Access Analyzer policy validation rejects it by default.
Long-lived keys? Legacy. Use roles: instance profiles, task roles, OIDC federation, SSO for humans.
SG vs NACL? SG: stateful, allow-only, per-ENI. NACL: stateless, supports deny, per-subnet, needs explicit ephemeral-port rules.
Why one NAT per AZ? A single NAT makes every private subnet depend on one AZ, and cross-AZ NAT traffic is charged.
Public subnet? Defined by a route to the IGW, not by a tag. Tags are human convention.
S3 strong consistency? Since Dec 2020 yes, for the current version. Derived systems, concurrent writes, and event delivery are still your problem.
S3 Standard-IA trap? 128 KiB minimum object size and a 30-day minimum; short-lived small objects cost more than Standard.
Presigned URL lifetime? Bounded by the assumed-role session, so generate per request; sign one key and one action.
Aurora vs RDS? Aurora for fast failover, fast PITR, storage that grows without downtime, many readers. RDS for engine completeness and lower steady cost.
Connection storms? Lambda/Fargate scale-out opens pools per replica. Use RDS Proxy/PgBouncer and set max_connections from memory.
Lambda concurrency model? One request per environment; concurrency = number of environments. That is the cold start equation.
Reserved concurrency trap? It is a cap *and* a claim on the account's 1,000 unreserved pool; over-reserving starves every other function.
CloudFront cache key? Path + configured headers/cookies/query. Missing Authorization in the key is a data leak; ignoring query strings serves the wrong variant.
SQS guarantees? At-least-once, unordered, duplicates expected. FIFO gives exactly-once processing within the dedup window.
Visibility timeout too short? Two consumers process the same message concurrently. Set it above worst-case processing (~6× function timeout) or renew it.
Batching saves money because? SQS/Lambda bill per *request*: 10 messages in one call costs a tenth of ten calls.
ECS circuit breaker? Rolls the deployment back automatically when tasks cannot reach steady state. The most valuable line in a service definition.
Why target_type = "ip" for Fargate? awsvpc mode gives tasks ENIs, so targets are registered by IP, not instance ID.

topics.title: Users and permissions
topics.description: Users and permissions within Linux Server Administration.
keyConcepts: The three account databases
A service account with ! or * in the shadow field cannot log in with a password; its shell is /usr/sbin/nologin.
Always lock the password (passwd -l) on service accounts, so sudo never offers them.
Creating accounts
File types
Mode bits
r=4, w=2, x=1. chmod 755 f = rwxr-xr-x, chmod 640 f = rw-r-----, chmod 600 f = owner only.
Symbolic form reads better: chmod u+x,g-w,o= deploy.sh, chmod -R u=rwX,g=rX,o= /srv/app.
X is capital on purpose: chmod -R a+X dir sets execute on directories and on files that already have execute for someone, so it does not make every data file executable.
Directories: x = traverse/enter, r = list names, w = create/remove entries. A directory with w but no x is useless and dangerous.
umask is subtracted from the base mode (files 666, dirs 777):
Ownership
commonMistakes: using -G instead of -aG in usermod (silently drops every other group); chmod -R 777 /srv "to fix permissions"; chown -R with a trailing symlink and no -h; chmod 600 then wondering why the *group* service account cannot read; adding an ACL entry but leaving the mask tight; leaving service accounts with a valid password or a bash shell; assuming uid 1000 means anything across two different machines; using -perm -4000 results without checking who owns the file.
practiceTasks: create a service account and a deploy account, put a shared file in an ACL-protected directory readable by two named users, prove that a third user cannot read it, show getfacl before and after removing an entry, and reproduce the setgid inheritance behaviour with touch.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain the difference between `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, and `/etc/group`. Which one holds password hashes?
What is umask, what does `022` produce, and how do you change it for a single command?
What do the setuid, setgid, and sticky bits do? Give a real example of each.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Setuid on a file makes the kernel run it with the file owner's uid, which is how passwd and sudo let an ordinary user do privileged work through a small, audited program instead of a root shell. Setgid on a file does the same for the group; on a directory it is a different feature entirely: new files inherit the directory's group and new subdirectories inherit setgid too, so a shared release directory keeps one group without anyone running chgrp. Sticky on a directory means only the owner of an entry or root can delete or rename it, which is why /tmp is 1777 and nobody can delete another user's files. The security warning is that any setuid binary you can replace is a root shell, so setuid files in world-writable directories are a pwn, and setuid shells are worse."

interviewQuestions.text: What is `X` in `chmod -R a+X /srv/app`, and why not `a+x`?
How do you give alice read+execute access to one file without changing its owner or making it world-readable?
What is the `mask` entry in an ACL, and what does `#effective:r--` mean in `getfacl` output?
`sudo usermod -G deploy alice` vs `-aG`. What did you just break?
Why create a separate service account per daemon instead of running everything as root or as `deploy`?
interviewQuestions.answer: "One account per daemon means the blast radius of a compromise is the daemon. A RCE in the image renderer gets the renderer's uid, so it cannot read /etc/shadow, cannot read the deploy user's SSH key, cannot write to /usr/bin, and cannot reach another service's socket. With everything as root, the same RCE is instantly root on the host. With everything as deploy, any one RCE also steals that account's SSH keys. Per-service accounts also give you clean audit logs, independent key rotation, and let you change one service's filesystem permissions without renegotiating access for everything. The cost is operational: you need the unit to declare the directories it may write to, and you must create log files and data dirs with matching ownership."

interviewQuestions.text: What does `find / -perm -4000` show, and why is a setuid binary in `/tmp` an emergency?
Directory `/srv/app/files` is `drwxrwsr-x` owned by `deploy:deploy`. You `su deploy` and create a file. Owner, group, and modes?
How do you lock an account without deleting it, and why lock service accounts?
What is `DynamicUser=yes` in systemd and what does it trade away?

topics.title: systemd and services
topics.description: systemd is PID 1 on a modern Linux host. It supervises processes, orders them, restarts them, watches their resources, controls their permissions, and collects their logs. It replaced SysVinit + upstart and is the answer to "who starts this thing and who restarts it when it dies".
keyConcepts: Unit types
Unit anatomy: a real service
The workflow you will actually use
systemctl edit is the habit worth forming
Type=notify and readiness
With Type=notify, systemd considers the unit *starting* until the process calls sd_notify(READY=1). Until then, dependent units wait and TimeoutStartSec applies.

Node has no built-in sd_notify, so you either use a small native module, write to the socket manually, or use Type=exec/simple and probe readiness yourself with a HEALTHCHECK-style ExecStartPost loop.
The payoff is honest readiness: nothing is routed to this instance until it says it is ready. The same problem, solved differently, is Kubernetes readiness probes (8.3).
Socket activation
systemd holds the listening socket, so a restart of the service causes zero dropped connections; the backlog is already open. nginx, sshd, Docker, and systemd's own journald socket all use this.
Accept=no (default) starts one service instance; Accept=yes starts one instance per connection.
Hardening and systemd-analyze security
commonMistakes: editing /lib/systemd/system/*.service instead of using systemctl edit drop-ins (updates overwrite it); forgetting daemon-reload after an edit; a unit file with CRLF line endings (systemd silently fails to parse parts of it); relying on Restart=always for a service that should stay down after a deploy; secrets in Environment= (visible via systemctl show to any user); TimeoutStopSec=15s for a service that drains for 30s (guaranteed SIGKILL mid-flush); assuming After= means "the dependency stays alive"; KillMode=control-group on a wrapper script that ignores SIGTERM.
practiceTasks: write a unit for a small Node service with ExecStartPre config validation, Restart=on-failure, rate limiting, a memory limit, and StateDirectory=; break it three times quickly and watch systemctl status report "start request repeated too quickly"; then tighten it with systemd-analyze security until the exposure is under 4.0, and finally replace it with a .timer + .service pair that runs a backup hourly with flock-based overlap protection.

interviewQuestions.text: Name the unit types and give one real use for each of service, socket, timer, target, slice.
Explain `After=` vs `Requires=` vs `Wants=`. Which one expresses "this needs the database up first"?
What does `Restart=on-failure` do, and why does it still not prevent a hot loop?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Restart=on-failure restarts the unit when the main process exits with a non-zero status, is killed by a signal other than SIGTERM and SIGINT, or hits a timeout. It is deliberately not unconditional: a clean exit during a deploy should stay stopped. The important detail is that systemd's backoff is flat, not exponential, so RestartSec=1s on a service that fails in 200ms will hammer the CPU and the logs 5 times a second forever. The thing that stops the loop is start rate limiting: StartLimitIntervalSec=60 with StartLimitBurst=5 makes the unit refuse to start again after five failures in a minute and enter a failed state, which is the behaviour you actually want, and which also means you must reset-failed before restarting after a fix."

interviewQuestions.text: What is the difference between `TimeoutStartSec`, `TimeoutStopSec`, and `RestartSec`?
Explain `Type=simple`, `Type=exec`, `Type=notify`, `Type=forking`, and `Type=oneshot`. Which one waits for a real readiness signal?
What does `KillMode=mixed` change, and why is `KillMode=control-group` dangerous for a shell that ignores signals?
Why is `ExecStartPre` better than chaining validation into `ExecStart`?
How do you override a packaged unit's settings durably, and how do you undo them?
What does `systemd-analyze security` measure, and which three directives move the score most?
What does `ProtectSystem=strict` actually do, and how does the service still write to its data directory?
List the secrets problems with `EnvironmentFile=` and the better alternatives.
interviewQuestions.answer: "EnvironmentFile puts a KEY=VALUE file on disk in plain text. It is better than a secret in git because ownership and mode can control it, mode 0640 root:appsvc, but it is still plaintext for root and for anyone in the service group, it is visible in the process environment of the running service, and it ends up in filesystem backups. Its format also surprises people: no export, no quotes, no variable expansion, no multiline values. The better options are, in order: a deploy tool that writes the file with 0600 ownership and never has it in git; systemd credentials, LoadCredentialEncrypted with systemd-creds, which encrypts at rest and binds decryption to the machine's boot state or TPM; and finally a secrets manager fetched at startup, which is the only option that supports rotation without a deploy."

interviewQuestions.text: Explain `StateDirectory=orders-api`. What does systemd create, and where?

topics.title: Firewalls
topics.description: a host firewall is one layer of network filtering, evaluated by the kernel's packet-filtering framework (nftables, with iptptables-nft compatibility) on rules you write. Its job is to reduce the number of reachable ports on a machine, so that a mistake in the application or in a security group has something else to fail against.
keyConcepts: Where filtering actually happens
ufw (Debian/Ubuntu)
firewalld (RHEL/Fedora/openSUSE), zone-based
Zone = a set of rules attached to an interface or a source subnet. The right mental model is "which trust zone is this traffic in", not "which ports do I like".
Defence in depth
IPv4 vs IPv6 parity — the asymmetry nobody tests
A host with global IPv6 reachable from the internet has a second front door. If your rules are IPv4-only, your "deny by default" is fiction.
Check what you have: ip -6 addr show scope global, ss -tlnp for tcp6/*:3000, ufw status should list [::]:22/tcp as well.
ufw: IPV6=yes in /etc/default/ufw (often no by default even when the kernel has IPv6).
nftables/firewalld: ip6tables-equivalents; firewalld families ipv4/ipv6 (--add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv6" ...').
netplan/cloud-init and most cloud SGs are IPv4-only by default; decide explicitly whether to use IPv6 or disable it, and test from outside both families.
net.ipv6.bindv6only=0 means an IPv4-mapped listener on :::3000 serves both families. Check with ss -4 -tlnp versus ss -6 -tlnp.
commonMistakes: enabling a firewall without an SSH allow rule (lockout, now needing the provider's console); ufw allow 22 after already being firewalled from a different source; forgetting the default-deny policy so rules are additive and you never audit the effective set; assuming cloud SGs make a host firewall redundant; IPv4-only rules on a dual-stack host; relying on Docker's default published-port behaviour to be firewalled; opening 3306/5432/6379 "temporarily" and never closing it.
practiceTasks: install ufw on a throwaway VM, deny inbound by default, allow SSH from your own address, and prove from a second machine that (a) 22 is reachable from you and (b) 5432 is not, then repeat with firewalld zones on a RHEL-family image, add an IPv6 test to show the parity failure, and demonstrate the Docker DOCKER-USER bypass and its fix.

interviewQuestions.text: Which two firewall tools ship with which distributions, and what is the underlying mechanism for both?
Write the ufw rules for: default-deny inbound, SSH limited to one source IP, Postgres only from the app subnet.
What does `ufw limit` do differently from `ufw allow`?
Why does a firewalld `--permanent` change not take effect until `--reload`, and what is the risk of the alternative (applying only at runtime)?
Explain firewalld zones and how traffic is assigned to one.
Why do you want a host firewall *and* a cloud security group? Give a concrete failure for each.
A service is bound to `0.0.0.0:3000` and is reachable from the internet. What is the firewall misconfiguration, and what is the application misconfiguration?
Your host has IPv6. What happens if your rules are IPv4-only, and how do you verify?
What is `IPV6=yes` in `/etc/default/ufw` and why is it often not set?
Explain `net.ipv6.bindv6only=0` and what a listener on `:::3000` means for IPv4 clients.
Docker publishes port 5432 and ufw still says `Deny`. Explain, and give two fixes.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Docker programs its own NAT and filter rules into the iptables/nftables chains and evaluates published ports ahead of, and instead of, the INPUT chain that ufw manages. Published container ports are DNAT'd and forwarded, so they never traverse ufw's rules, and a ufw deny 5432 is silently ineffective. Two real fixes: either insert rules into the DOCKER-USER chain, which Docker creates specifically so administrators can filter forwarded container traffic, or publish on loopback only with -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432, so the port is not reachable from any external interface at all. The second is strictly better when the only client is on the same host."

interviewQuestions.text: What is the `DOCKER-USER` chain for?

topics.title: SSH hardening
topics.description: SSH is an encrypted remote shell that, in practice, is the entire access-control surface of a production host. Hardening it is the highest-value security work a backend or DevOps engineer does, and sshd_config plus authorized_keys are where that work is visible.
keyConcepts: Key-based authentication
The private key never leaves your machine and must be 0600. ssh-agent holds decrypted keys in memory so you do not retype a passphrase:
Rotation: keep two keys, distribute the new one, remove the old line, then verify. Rotating a password does not revoke keys; offboarding means removing the authorized_keys line or the account.
authorized_keys permissions (StrictModes)
Any group/other write bit on $HOME, ~/.ssh, or authorized_keys makes sshd refuse the file. This is StrictModes yes and it is correct.
authorized_keys options (real, and worth using)

restrict = no port forwarding, no agent forwarding, no X11, no PTY allocation. expiry-time="YYYYMMDD" (OpenSSH 9.2+) makes the key stop working on its own. command="..." forces every session through a wrapper, which is how you turn SSH into a controlled deployment channel.
sshd_config hardening
sudo sshd -t then reload, never restart, and never edit before you have a fallback path (provider console, serial console, or a second session).
PasswordAuthentication no does not disable password auth for keyboard-interactive PAM flows; you need KbdInteractiveAuthentication no too (and AuthenticationMethods publickey overrides everything).
fail2ban (or a cloud IDS) on top bans repeated failed logins from rotating IPs; ufw limit 22/tcp is the cheap version.
~/.ssh/config: aliases
commonMistakes: editing sshd_config and running systemctl restart ssh on the only open session (one typo and you are locked out); PasswordAuthentication no without KbdInteractiveAuthentication no and discovering MFA prompts still work; chmod 644 authorized_keys "so it is readable" (sshd refuses it, or worse, accepts it after StrictModes no and you have an attack surface); committing a private key to a repo; ssh -L 5432:... with no bind address on a public network; forwarding the agent "just this once"; accept-new and then blindly running ssh-keygen -R for every change warning you see.
practiceTasks: create a throwaway VM, move SSH to a high port, disable password and root login, add two keys with a from= restriction and an expiry, harden sshd_config with systemd-analyze-style verification (sshd -t), tunnel to a Postgres that only listens on loopback, and finally test that ProxyJump works while ForwardAgent yes is *not* set.

interviewQuestions.text: Walk through setting up key-based auth from scratch, including every permission that must be right and the error sshd gives when one is wrong.
Why do you need `KbdInteractiveAuthentication no` in addition to `PasswordAuthentication no`?
What does `StrictModes yes` actually check?
Explain `PermitRootLogin no` vs `prohibit-password` vs `yes`.
What do the `from=`, `command=`, `restrict`, and `expiry-time` options in `authorized_keys` do?
Why does rotating a user's password not revoke their SSH access?
Write a hardened `sshd_config` for a bastion host that still needs port forwarding for developers.
What is `Match`, and what is the gotcha about where it can appear in the file?
You need to reach `db.internal:5432` from your laptop with only access to `bastion`. Give the command and the psql invocation.
What is the danger of `ssh -L 5432:db:5432` without a bind address?
What does `ExitOnForwardFailure=yes` protect you from?
Explain `ProxyJump` versus `-J` versus `ProxyCommand` versus `ForwardAgent`. Which one keeps your keys off the intermediate host?
interviewQuestions.answer: "ProxyJump and -J are the same thing, -J being the shorthand, and both open a real SSH session to the intermediate host which then forwards a channel to the target; your key is only ever used against the jump host and against the target from your own machine. ProxyCommand is the general form underneath it, and you can use it for things SSH cannot express natively, such as a wireguard tunnel or a serial console. Agent forwarding is the one to distrust: it exports your local agent to the remote host so it can authenticate onward, which means anyone who compromises that host can use every key loaded in your agent, including your personal key, against every host those keys are authorized on, for as long as you stay connected. Use ProxyJump and never forward the agent."

topics.title: Process monitoring
topics.description: the small set of tools that turn "the box feels slow" into a specific bottleneck. You do not need a monitoring platform to start: uptime, free, vmstat, iostat, ss, and top are on every machine, and knowing their four important columns each is a genuine senior skill.
keyConcepts: Load average

Load average is not CPU percent. It is the exponentially-averaged count of tasks that are running or runnable (on a CPU run queue) or in uninterruptible sleep (D), sampled once a minute, shown as 1/5/15-minute averages.
Interpretation on a 4-CPU box: load 4 = fully utilised; load 8 = 2x oversubscribed and latency is rising; load 1 on 4 CPUs = 25% utilised.
Load high with idle CPU = not CPU-bound. Look for D state (storage/NFS), heavy swapping (vmstat si/so), or a run-queue full of processes blocked on I/O.
Load 0 with a hung service is possible: a process blocked in a deadlock-free select() forever contributes nothing.
Load rising over 15 min but flat over 1 min means the problem started recently; the shape of the three numbers tells you when.
Memory, and the false comfort of caching

Linux uses free memory for page cache and reclaims it under pressure. So low free is healthy; the number to watch is available (and MemAvailable in /proc/meminfo), which estimates how much can be handed out without swapping.
used in free (older versions) double-counted or hid cache, which is why scripts should use available.
buff/cache breakdown: Buffers = block I/O buffers; Cached = page cache for file reads; Shmem = tmpfs.

Reclaim pressure, not exhaustion, is the real signal: /proc/pressure/memory (some avg10=0.00 avg60=1.84 avg300=0.72 total=...) says what fraction of the time tasks were stalled waiting for memory. A growing avg60 matters even with plenty free.
MemoryHigh (soft, throttle and reclaim) versus MemoryMax (hard, OOM-kill) is the distinction to carry into 8.2.
commonMistakes: reading load average as a percentage of CPU; alerting on free memory instead of available or PSI; trusting %util on NVMe or RAID arrays; tuning tcp_fin_timeout down aggressively to "fix" TIME-WAIT (it breaks long-lived connections); treating CLOSE-WAIT as normal; running iostat once without an interval and drawing conclusions from the since-boot average; ignoring st on virtual machines and concluding the app is slow; using netstat instead of ss on a machine with tens of thousands of sockets; turning off swap "because Linux manages memory better" on a 512 MB VM.
practiceTasks: saturate a VM four ways (a busy loop, a memory hog, an fsync loop, and a fork bomb guarded by ulimit) and record uptime, free, vmstat 1 5, and iostat -x 1 for each, then write the diagnosis for each from those four commands alone. Then open 20 000 sockets to a dead port and drive CLOSE-WAIT to see the leak.

interviewQuestions.text: What exactly is the load average, and what does it count besides running processes?
Load average is 12 on a 4-CPU box and CPU idle is 70%. Where do you look, and what commands prove it?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Load 12 on 4 CPUs with 70% idle means the run queues are not full of CPU work, so the load number is counting something else. The most common cause is tasks in uninterruptible sleep, which the kernel includes in the load average because they are queued work that cannot proceed. So the first command is to look for D-state processes with ps -eo stat,pid,cmd | awk '$1 ~ /^D/', then iostat -xz 1 to see await and queue depth, and dmesg -T | tail for device errors or a hung NFS mount. The other possibility is thrashing, in which case vmstat 1 5 shows non-zero si and so columns, meaning processes are being pushed to swap and pulled back. A third possibility is that the run queue is full of tasks blocked on a lock rather than on CPU, which shows up as threads stuck in the same wait when you take a thread dump."

topics.title: Disk and memory troubleshooting
topics.description: "disk full" and "server slow" have a small number of real causes and a documented order for finding them. The most important habit is knowing which commands answer which question, because the wrong command sends you down a one-hour path.
keyConcepts: df vs du
df reports filesystem usage (blocks). du reports disk usage of files as seen from a directory, and it counts hard-linked files once but follows bind mounts, so it can double-count across filesystems.
The gap (188G vs 142G) means blocks are held by files du cannot see: files that were deleted while a process still has them open, other mounts, or filesystem metadata and reserved blocks.
Deleted-but-open files: the classic
The file is unlinked (name gone) but the inode lives until every open descriptor and mapping is closed. df sees the blocks; du does not.

Fix, best first: make the holder reopen or restart it (logrotate + reopen, or systemctl restart rsyslog). Immediate space reclamation without a restart: : > /proc/1102/fd/7 (works for regular files, not sockets) — but you have just thrown away the log content.
Same class of problem with Docker json-file logs, rotated-but-still-open files, deleted VMs with held snapshots, and lsof on NFS.
Inodes

ENOSPC with free space and 100% inodes means millions of tiny files: a mail spool, a session-file cache, an application writing one file per event, or a build artefact directory. df -i is the command people forget.
df -hT shows filesystem type, which matters when you plan fixes.
Disks, mounts, and filesystems
Mount options worth knowing: noatime (huge for read-heavy workloads, standard on servers), relatime, discard (TRIM), nofail (boot even if the disk is missing), ro.
commonMistakes: running rm -rf before lsof +L1 (deleting more files and making recovery worse); restarting every service hoping one of them fixes it; kill -9 on an OOM victim repeatedly without finding the leak; assuming low MemFree means a memory problem; setting swappiness=0 and calling a thrashing host fixed; df -h without -T and not knowing what filesystem you are on; deleting files by atime with noatime enabled (they are never updated, so the logic is wrong); skipping journalctl -k because "the app logs look fine".
practiceTasks: create a 200 MB loopback filesystem, fill it with a file, delete it while a process holds it open, show df vs du, reclaim it, then generate an inode exhaustion case with 100 000 empty files, and finally run the full 10-step triage against a deliberately broken host (CPU hog + a stalled mount + an OOM-limited service) and write up the timeline.

interviewQuestions.text: `df` says 96% full, `du` says 46% used. List every possible cause and the command that proves each.
interviewQuestions.answer: "There are four real explanations. One: a file was deleted while a process still holds it open, so the inode keeps the blocks and df counts them while du cannot see the name; lsof +L1 lists them and restarting or truncating the holder reclaims the space. Two: another filesystem is mounted inside the tree that du is either following or not, so du/df disagree in both directions; lsblk -f and mount, or du with --one-file-system, settle it. Three: filesystem reserved blocks or metadata overhead, which show up as overhead in df and in tune2fs -l. Four: hidden data in another location entirely, Docker's overlay2 layers, deleted VM snapshots, or a partition that df sums into / but du cannot walk because it is not mounted. In practice the first two account for nearly everything, and lsof +L1 is the first command to run."

topics.title: Users, groups, and permissions
topics.description: Users, groups, and permissions within Linux Server Administration.
keyConcepts: The three account databases
A service account with ! or * in the shadow field cannot log in with a password; its shell is /usr/sbin/nologin.
Always lock the password (passwd -l) on service accounts, so sudo never offers them.
Creating accounts
File types
Mode bits
r=4, w=2, x=1. chmod 755 f = rwxr-xr-x, chmod 640 f = rw-r-----, chmod 600 f = owner only.
Symbolic form reads better: chmod u+x,g-w,o= deploy.sh, chmod -R u=rwX,g=rX,o= /srv/app.
X is capital on purpose: chmod -R a+X dir sets execute on directories and on files that already have execute for someone, so it does not make every data file executable.
Directories: x = traverse/enter, r = list names, w = create/remove entries. A directory with w but no x is useless and dangerous.
umask is subtracted from the base mode (files 666, dirs 777):
Ownership
commonMistakes: using -G instead of -aG in usermod (silently drops every other group); chmod -R 777 /srv "to fix permissions"; chown -R with a trailing symlink and no -h; chmod 600 then wondering why the *group* service account cannot read; adding an ACL entry but leaving the mask tight; leaving service accounts with a valid password or a bash shell; assuming uid 1000 means anything across two different machines; using -perm -4000 results without checking who owns the file.
practiceTasks: create a service account and a deploy account, put a shared file in an ACL-protected directory readable by two named users, prove that a third user cannot read it, show getfacl before and after removing an entry, and reproduce the setgid inheritance behaviour with touch.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain the difference between `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, and `/etc/group`. Which one holds password hashes?
What is umask, what does `022` produce, and how do you change it for a single command?
What do the setuid, setgid, and sticky bits do? Give a real example of each.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Setuid on a file makes the kernel run it with the file owner's uid, which is how passwd and sudo let an ordinary user do privileged work through a small, audited program instead of a root shell. Setgid on a file does the same for the group; on a directory it is a different feature entirely: new files inherit the directory's group and new subdirectories inherit setgid too, so a shared release directory keeps one group without anyone running chgrp. Sticky on a directory means only the owner of an entry or root can delete or rename it, which is why /tmp is 1777 and nobody can delete another user's files. The security warning is that any setuid binary you can replace is a root shell, so setuid files in world-writable directories are a pwn, and setuid shells are worse."

interviewQuestions.text: What is `X` in `chmod -R a+X /srv/app`, and why not `a+x`?
How do you give alice read+execute access to one file without changing its owner or making it world-readable?
What is the `mask` entry in an ACL, and what does `#effective:r--` mean in `getfacl` output?
`sudo usermod -G deploy alice` vs `-aG`. What did you just break?
Why create a separate service account per daemon instead of running everything as root or as `deploy`?
interviewQuestions.answer: "One account per daemon means the blast radius of a compromise is the daemon. A RCE in the image renderer gets the renderer's uid, so it cannot read /etc/shadow, cannot read the deploy user's SSH key, cannot write to /usr/bin, and cannot reach another service's socket. With everything as root, the same RCE is instantly root on the host. With everything as deploy, any one RCE also steals that account's SSH keys. Per-service accounts also give you clean audit logs, independent key rotation, and let you change one service's filesystem permissions without renegotiating access for everything. The cost is operational: you need the unit to declare the directories it may write to, and you must create log files and data dirs with matching ownership."

interviewQuestions.text: What does `find / -perm -4000` show, and why is a setuid binary in `/tmp` an emergency?

How do you lock an account without deleting it, and why lock service accounts?
What is `DynamicUser=yes` in systemd and what does it trade away?
