topics.title: Processes, signals, and inspection
topics.description: Processes, signals, and inspection within Linux Server Administration.
keyConcepts: Seeing processes
Process states (STAT)

D state is the single most useful clue in process triage. A D process cannot be killed, even with SIGKILL, until the I/O completes. A pile of D processes with load average climbing and CPU sitting at 5% means the box is blocked on storage or a hung NFS mount, not on CPU. Confirm with ps -eo stat,cmd | awk '$1 ~ /D/' and iostat -x 1.

Zombies hold a PID slot and an entry in the process table, but no memory. They only persist because their parent has not called wait(). Fixed by fixing the parent: a service that ignores its children's exit codes, or a program that forks without reaping. Never "fix" a zombie by killing it; it is already dead.
Parent/child and orphans
PPID is the parent PID. When a parent dies, orphans are re-parented to PID 1 (/sbin/init on a host, your entrypoint inside a container).

PID 1 is special in the kernel: signals with a default action are not delivered unless PID 1 installed a handler, and PID 1 must reap children or zombies accumulate. That is why containers need an init (--init, tini, dumb-init) or an app that handles both.
ps -ef | grep defunct finds zombies; ps -o stat,ppid,cmd -p <zombie ppid> identifies the guilty parent.
Signals

SIGKILL semantics: the kernel terminates the process immediately. No handler runs, so no flush, no connection close, no temp-file cleanup, no finally blocks, no buffer writes. Flushing data from a 4 GB in-memory queue can take tens of seconds, and losing it corrupts state. SIGSTOP/SIGKILL are the only two signals the kernel refuses to let you catch, block, or ignore.
SIGTERM is a request. Correct handling: stop accepting new connections, finish or fail in-flight work within a deadline, close DB pools and flush logs, exit 0.
Must stay under the supervisor's stop deadline: TimeoutStopSec=45s in systemd, stopGracePeriodSeconds in Kubernetes, Compose stop_grace_period.
commonMistakes: reaching for kill -9 first (you lose buffered writes and leave locks behind); killing the shell instead of the process tree (pkill -f node may hit your own session); assuming a service dies instantly on systemctl stop (it gets SIGTERM and then SIGKILL after TimeoutStopSec); confusing a zombie with a memory leak; using ps aux | grep without grep -v grep; sending signals to PID numbers you read from a stale ps; forgetting SIGKILL does not run cleanup handlers that other services rely on (distributed locks, sessions).
practiceTasks: write a Node service that handles SIGTERM with a 20-second drain and logs its phases; start it with nohup, then with setsid; kill -9 it during a request and show the difference in logs; create a zombie deliberately (fork without reaping) and reap it; and use strace -c to prove which syscall a blocking endpoint spends its time in.

interviewQuestions.text: What is `D` state and why can you not `kill -9` a process in it?
interviewQuestions.answer: "D is uninterruptible sleep: the task is blocked in a kernel path that cannot be interrupted, which historically means a device or filesystem operation. The kill syscall still records the signal as pending, but the task is not at a point where signals are delivered, so the process looks unkillable until the I/O completes. Operationally it is the classic fingerprint of a storage problem: high load average with almost no CPU usage, because load average counts runnable tasks plus tasks in uninterruptible sleep. So the first move with runaway load and idle CPU is ps -eo stat,cmd to find the D tasks, then iostat -x 1 and dmesg -T | tail to look at the device and for hung NFS mounts."

interviewQuestions.text: What exactly does `SIGKILL` skip that `SIGTERM` does?
Walk through `nohup`, `disown`, and `setsid`: which signal does each ignore, and which one actually detaches the process?
A process shows `Z`. What is happening, what does it cost, and what fixes it?
Why do daemons need a `SIGTERM` handler, and how do you pick the timeout?
Read this `ps` line: `PID 2318 PPID 1 STAT Ssl`. What do the four `STAT` characters mean, and why is `PPID 1` significant?
`ls -l /proc/2318/fd` shows `5 -> socket:[4218871]`. How do you turn that into a useful answer?
What does `strace -f -ttT` add over plain `strace`, and when would `-c` be more useful than a per-line trace?
How do you find the real command line of a process when `ps aux | grep node` gives you your own grep?
A service is using far more memory than expected. What do you compare in `/proc/<pid>/status` and `smaps_rollup`?
Explain `nohup`, `setsid` and systemd as three answers to "run this in the background and keep it alive". Which one do you actually ship?
interviewQuestions.answer: "nohup only sets SIGHUP to ignore, so the process survives you closing the terminal, but it is still a child of your shell, it still dies on reboot, and if it crashes nothing restarts it. disown just removes it from the shell's job table; it does not change signal handling at all. setsid creates a new session and process group with no controlling terminal, so Ctrl+C no longer reaches it, which is a genuinely detached process. All three are hacks for interactive work. For anything that must stay up I ship a systemd unit, because it gives restart with backoff, resource limits, structured logging, ordered dependencies, start rate limiting, and boot-time startup — none of which a shell trick gives you."

```js
// Node: graceful shutdown, the shape every service should have
let shuttingDown = false;
async function shutdown(signal) {
  if (shuttingDown) return;
  shuttingDown = true;
  logger.info({ signal }, 'draining');
  const force = setTimeout(() => {
    logger.error('graceful shutdown timed out, forcing exit');
    process.exit(1);
  }, 25_000);
  force.unref();
  server.close(async () => {          // no new connections accepted
    await pool.end();                 // DB pool drained
    await logger.flush?.();
    clearTimeout(force);
    process.exit(0);
  });
}
process.on('SIGTERM', () => shutdown('SIGTERM'));
process.on('SIGINT', () => shutdown('SIGINT'));
```

topics.title: systemd
topics.description: systemd is PID 1 on a modern Linux host. It supervises processes, orders them, restarts them, watches their resources, controls their permissions, and collects their logs. It replaced SysVinit + upstart and is the answer to "who starts this thing and who restarts it when it dies".
keyConcepts: Unit types
Unit anatomy: a real service
The workflow you will actually use
systemctl edit is the habit worth forming
Type=notify and readiness
With Type=notify, systemd considers the unit *starting* until the process calls sd_notify(READY=1). Until then, dependent units wait and TimeoutStartSec applies.

Node has no built-in sd_notify, so you either use a small native module, write to the socket manually, or use Type=exec/simple and probe readiness yourself with a HEALTHCHECK-style ExecStartPost loop.
The payoff is honest readiness: nothing is routed to this instance until it says it is ready. The same problem, solved differently, is Kubernetes readiness probes (8.3).
Socket activation
systemd holds the listening socket, so a restart of the service causes zero dropped connections; the backlog is already open. nginx, sshd, Docker, and systemd's own journald socket all use this.
Accept=no (default) starts one service instance; Accept=yes starts one instance per connection.
Hardening and systemd-analyze security
commonMistakes: editing /lib/systemd/system/*.service instead of using systemctl edit drop-ins (updates overwrite it); forgetting daemon-reload after an edit; a unit file with CRLF line endings (systemd silently fails to parse parts of it); relying on Restart=always for a service that should stay down after a deploy; secrets in Environment= (visible via systemctl show to any user); TimeoutStopSec=15s for a service that drains for 30s (guaranteed SIGKILL mid-flush); assuming After= means "the dependency stays alive"; KillMode=control-group on a wrapper script that ignores SIGTERM.
practiceTasks: write a unit for a small Node service with ExecStartPre config validation, Restart=on-failure, rate limiting, a memory limit, and StateDirectory=; break it three times quickly and watch systemctl status report "start request repeated too quickly"; then tighten it with systemd-analyze security until the exposure is under 4.0, and finally replace it with a .timer + .service pair that runs a backup hourly with flock-based overlap protection.

interviewQuestions.text: Name the unit types and give one real use for each of service, socket, timer, target, slice.
Explain `After=` vs `Requires=` vs `Wants=`. Which one expresses "this needs the database up first"?
What does `Restart=on-failure` do, and why does it still not prevent a hot loop?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Restart=on-failure restarts the unit when the main process exits with a non-zero status, is killed by a signal other than SIGTERM and SIGINT, or hits a timeout. It is deliberately not unconditional: a clean exit during a deploy should stay stopped. The important detail is that systemd's backoff is flat, not exponential, so RestartSec=1s on a service that fails in 200ms will hammer the CPU and the logs 5 times a second forever. The thing that stops the loop is start rate limiting: StartLimitIntervalSec=60 with StartLimitBurst=5 makes the unit refuse to start again after five failures in a minute and enter a failed state, which is the behaviour you actually want, and which also means you must reset-failed before restarting after a fix."

interviewQuestions.text: What is the difference between `TimeoutStartSec`, `TimeoutStopSec`, and `RestartSec`?
Explain `Type=simple`, `Type=exec`, `Type=notify`, `Type=forking`, and `Type=oneshot`. Which one waits for a real readiness signal?
What does `KillMode=mixed` change, and why is `KillMode=control-group` dangerous for a shell that ignores signals?
Why is `ExecStartPre` better than chaining validation into `ExecStart`?
How do you override a packaged unit's settings durably, and how do you undo them?
What does `systemd-analyze security` measure, and which three directives move the score most?
What does `ProtectSystem=strict` actually do, and how does the service still write to its data directory?
List the secrets problems with `EnvironmentFile=` and the better alternatives.
interviewQuestions.answer: "EnvironmentFile puts a KEY=VALUE file on disk in plain text. It is better than a secret in git because ownership and mode can control it, mode 0640 root:appsvc, but it is still plaintext for root and for anyone in the service group, it is visible in the process environment of the running service, and it ends up in filesystem backups. Its format also surprises people: no export, no quotes, no variable expansion, no multiline values. The better options are, in order: a deploy tool that writes the file with 0600 ownership and never has it in git; systemd credentials, LoadCredentialEncrypted with systemd-creds, which encrypts at rest and binds decryption to the machine's boot state or TPM; and finally a secrets manager fetched at startup, which is the only option that supports rotation without a deploy."

topics.title: Logs and journald
topics.description: logs are the only record of what a system actually did. On a modern host they come from journald (structured, binary, indexed) and from files written by applications; both need a retention policy, a size policy, and an off-box destination, because a log pipeline that fills the disk takes the application down with it.
keyConcepts: The three output streams a server writes to
journald levels (syslog priorities)
journald fields (this is why journal beats flat files)

The underscore fields are trusted: journald sets them from the process's credentials and the kernel, not from what the app claims. SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER is app-provided. That distinction is what makes journal queries trustworthy when auditing.
_BOOT_ID is how you scope a query to one boot and why -b -1 (previous boot) is a real command.
journalctl, the commands worth memorising
journald configuration: /etc/systemd/journald.conf
Storage=volatile (the default on most systemd versions) means a reboot erases all logs. That is the single most common reason "I have no logs for the incident". Storage=persistent fixes it.
SystemKeepFree is the safety valve. Without it, journald will happily consume every free byte. Set a hard cap plus a floor you refuse to cross.

Rate limiting silently drops messages when a service exceeds RateLimitBurst, and emits "Suppressed N messages". That is why a log storm looks like it stopped: journalctl | grep Suppressed and then fix the storm's rate, not the drop.
A real logrotate config

copytruncate vs create + reopen. create/default mode renames the live file and creates a new one, which is atomic and lossless but your app is still holding the old file descriptor, so it keeps writing to the renamed file forever. You must make the app reopen (SIGHUP, or a logger that watches the inode). copytruncate avoids the reopen requirement at the cost of a small loss window and doubled I/O. For a high-volume Node logger, prefer a rotating stream library or copytruncate and measure the gap.
commonMistakes: assuming logs survive reboot without Storage=persistent; setting rotate 30 daily with no size cap on a noisy service; create 0644 root root for an app's log so the app loses write access at rotation; compress without delaycompress and no reload hook; using tail -f on a rotated file (you follow the old inode forever, tail -F is safer); grepping journalctl for a PID that has been recycled; shipping logs with no retention policy; putting request bodies (with PII or tokens) into logs at info level; treating a log line as evidence when the log pipeline dropped messages.
practiceTasks: enable persistent journald with a 1 GB cap, restart a service in a loop until start request repeated too many times appears, then count the suppressed messages, write a logrotate block for a high-volume app and prove the reopen behaviour by watching the inode change, and ship one host's logs to a second machine over rsyslog with a disk-spill queue.

interviewQuestions.text: What is journald, and which fields in a journal record are trusted versus app-supplied?
Give the exact `journalctl` command for: follow one unit's logs; only errors in the last 30 minutes; this boot's kernel errors; the previous boot; a specific PID; the last 500 lines in a script.
Why does `journalctl -u x -f` show nothing after a reboot? What single directive fixes it?
interviewQuestions.answer: "The reason logs vanish across reboots is that journald defaults to Storage=volatile, which keeps everything in a RAM-backed file under /run and throws it away when the machine boots. You confirm it with journalctl --disk-usage showing only a small active journal, or by journalctl --list-boots having exactly one entry. The fix is Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf, which puts journals under /var/log/journal/<machine-id>, followed by a systemctl restart systemd-journald and, on a systemd version that needs it, a mkdir of /var/log/journal. While you are there you also set SystemMaxUse and SystemKeepFree so persistent logs cannot become the reason the disk fills."

interviewQuestions.text: Explain `_BOOT_ID` and what `-b -1` is for.
What does `RateLimitBurst` do, and how do you prove messages were dropped?
Explain `Storage=persistent` vs `Storage=volatile` vs `Storage=auto`.
What is `SystemKeepFree` for, and what happens without it?
When do you need `logrotate` if your app logs to stdout and systemd collects it?
Compare `copytruncate` with `create` plus a reopen signal. Which loses data, and in what window?
interviewQuestions.answer: "copytruncate copies the live file to app.log.1 and then truncates app.log to zero, keeping the same inode, so the application can keep writing to the file descriptor it already has without reopening. The loss window is between the copy finishing and the truncate, during which anything the app writes is thrown away, and it is worse on a high-volume file. The create mode renames app.log to app.log.1 and creates a brand new app.log, which is atomic and lossless, but the running process still holds the old inode and will keep writing into app.log.1 forever unless you make it reopen. So create plus a reopen signal is correct when you control the application; copytruncate is the pragmatic choice when you do not, and you should quantify the window with a log rate estimate before choosing it."

interviewQuestions.text: What does `create 0640 appsvc appsvc` in a logrotate block prevent?
Write a logrotate block for a 2 GB/day log that must keep 30 days compressed. What is wrong with it?

topics.title: Cron and scheduled jobs
topics.description: cron is the original scheduler: a daemon that wakes every minute and runs whatever the crontabs say. It is still the right answer for "run this on a schedule on this host", and the wrong answer for anything you need to observe, retry, or alert on.
keyConcepts: Format
Special strings
The cron environment pitfalls that will bite you
PATH is minimal. Not your login shell's PATH, and not nvm's. npm, node, python3 under ~/.nvm or ~/.asdf are invisible. Fix: absolute paths in the command, or set PATH= at the top of the crontab.
SHELL=/bin/sh on Debian/Ubuntu, which is dash, not bash. Bashisms ([[ ]], source, arrays, =~) fail with confusing errors.
No TERM, no DISPLAY, and a minimal environment generally; HOME is set to the cron user's home.
% is special: everything after the first % on a command line is fed to the command's stdin as newlines. date +\%Y-\%m-\%d must escape it.
Multi-line commands need backslash continuations, and a trailing comment in a crontab after a command breaks that command.
MAILTO: output is mailed on completion. With no MTA installed the mail goes nowhere and you find out from the absence of a report. Always redirect and log.
Overlapping runs: cron starts the next occurrence regardless of whether the last one finished. A 10-minute backup in a */15 schedule runs concurrently, twice a day overlapping.
Overlap prevention and correct ownership
systemd timers, the modern replacement
commonMistakes: relative paths and ~ in crontabs (cron does not source your rc files, and ~ needs to be spelled out or $HOME used); relying on npm/node/python from nvm; 0 3 * * * cmd1 ; cmd2 where cmd2 always runs; no redirection so output vanishes; chmod +x on a script whose first line is not a valid interpreter path (plus the "noexec" mount trap); editing /etc/crontab when you meant a user crontab (it has an extra user column); a cron job with no lock in /etc/cron.d for a stateful job; assuming a job that never ran will ever tell you.
practiceTasks: write a crontab job plus a systemd timer that perform the same backup, show that the cron version fails in a minimal environment while the timer version inherits its unit's environment, demonstrate the overlap problem and then fix it with flock, and add an OnFailure unit so a deliberately failing job pages you.

interviewQuestions.text: Write the crontab line for every 5 minutes, every weekday at 08:30, and the first day of each month at 00:15.
A crontab job works in your shell but fails under cron with `node: command not found`. Why, and what are the two fixes?
What is `SHELL` in cron's environment on Debian/Ubuntu, and what breaks because of it?
Why is `%` special in a crontab, and how do you use `date +%Y`?
What happens to the mail a crontab job produces when `MAILTO` is unset or there is no MTA?
Your hourly job takes 90 minutes. What happens, and what are two ways to stop it?
interviewQuestions.answer: "cron fires the next occurrence one minute after the previous one starts, regardless of whether the previous run has finished, so an hourly job that takes ninety minutes overlaps for half an hour, and with retries or a larger backlog it can stack many concurrent copies fighting over the same resources. Two fixes: take a non-blocking lock so a second invocation exits immediately, which is the exec 9>/run/lock/job.lock plus flock -n 9 pattern and exits 0 so cron does not report failure; and use a systemd timer with OnUnitInactiveSec instead of OnUnitActiveSec, which schedules the next run relative to when the last one finished, so a slow job naturally stretches the schedule rather than overlapping it."

interviewQuestions.text: Show how to prevent overlap with `flock`, both in a shell script and in a systemd unit.

topics.title: SSH
topics.description: SSH is an encrypted remote shell that, in practice, is the entire access-control surface of a production host. Hardening it is the highest-value security work a backend or DevOps engineer does, and sshd_config plus authorized_keys are where that work is visible.
keyConcepts: Key-based authentication
The private key never leaves your machine and must be 0600. ssh-agent holds decrypted keys in memory so you do not retype a passphrase:
Rotation: keep two keys, distribute the new one, remove the old line, then verify. Rotating a password does not revoke keys; offboarding means removing the authorized_keys line or the account.
authorized_keys permissions (StrictModes)
Any group/other write bit on $HOME, ~/.ssh, or authorized_keys makes sshd refuse the file. This is StrictModes yes and it is correct.
authorized_keys options (real, and worth using)

restrict = no port forwarding, no agent forwarding, no X11, no PTY allocation. expiry-time="YYYYMMDD" (OpenSSH 9.2+) makes the key stop working on its own. command="..." forces every session through a wrapper, which is how you turn SSH into a controlled deployment channel.
sshd_config hardening
sudo sshd -t then reload, never restart, and never edit before you have a fallback path (provider console, serial console, or a second session).
PasswordAuthentication no does not disable password auth for keyboard-interactive PAM flows; you need KbdInteractiveAuthentication no too (and AuthenticationMethods publickey overrides everything).
fail2ban (or a cloud IDS) on top bans repeated failed logins from rotating IPs; ufw limit 22/tcp is the cheap version.
~/.ssh/config: aliases
commonMistakes: editing sshd_config and running systemctl restart ssh on the only open session (one typo and you are locked out); PasswordAuthentication no without KbdInteractiveAuthentication no and discovering MFA prompts still work; chmod 644 authorized_keys "so it is readable" (sshd refuses it, or worse, accepts it after StrictModes no and you have an attack surface); committing a private key to a repo; ssh -L 5432:... with no bind address on a public network; forwarding the agent "just this once"; accept-new and then blindly running ssh-keygen -R for every change warning you see.
practiceTasks: create a throwaway VM, move SSH to a high port, disable password and root login, add two keys with a from= restriction and an expiry, harden sshd_config with systemd-analyze-style verification (sshd -t), tunnel to a Postgres that only listens on loopback, and finally test that ProxyJump works while ForwardAgent yes is *not* set.

interviewQuestions.text: Walk through setting up key-based auth from scratch, including every permission that must be right and the error sshd gives when one is wrong.
Why do you need `KbdInteractiveAuthentication no` in addition to `PasswordAuthentication no`?

What is the danger of `ssh -L 5432:db:5432` without a bind address?
What does `ExitOnForwardFailure=yes` protect you from?
Explain `ProxyJump` versus `-J` versus `ProxyCommand` versus `ForwardAgent`. Which one keeps your keys off the intermediate host?
interviewQuestions.answer: "ProxyJump and -J are the same thing, -J being the shorthand, and both open a real SSH session to the intermediate host which then forwards a channel to the target; your key is only ever used against the jump host and against the target from your own machine. ProxyCommand is the general form underneath it, and you can use it for things SSH cannot express natively, such as a wireguard tunnel or a serial console. Agent forwarding is the one to distrust: it exports your local agent to the remote host so it can authenticate onward, which means anyone who compromises that host can use every key loaded in your agent, including your personal key, against every host those keys are authorized on, for as long as you stay connected. Use ProxyJump and never forward the agent."

topics.title: Process and resource monitoring
topics.description: the small set of tools that turn "the box feels slow" into a specific bottleneck. You do not need a monitoring platform to start: uptime, free, vmstat, iostat, ss, and top are on every machine, and knowing their four important columns each is a genuine senior skill.
keyConcepts: Load average

Load average is not CPU percent. It is the exponentially-averaged count of tasks that are running or runnable (on a CPU run queue) or in uninterruptible sleep (D), sampled once a minute, shown as 1/5/15-minute averages.
Interpretation on a 4-CPU box: load 4 = fully utilised; load 8 = 2x oversubscribed and latency is rising; load 1 on 4 CPUs = 25% utilised.
Load high with idle CPU = not CPU-bound. Look for D state (storage/NFS), heavy swapping (vmstat si/so), or a run-queue full of processes blocked on I/O.
Load 0 with a hung service is possible: a process blocked in a deadlock-free select() forever contributes nothing.
Load rising over 15 min but flat over 1 min means the problem started recently; the shape of the three numbers tells you when.
Memory, and the false comfort of caching

Linux uses free memory for page cache and reclaims it under pressure. So low free is healthy; the number to watch is available (and MemAvailable in /proc/meminfo), which estimates how much can be handed out without swapping.
used in free (older versions) double-counted or hid cache, which is why scripts should use available.
buff/cache breakdown: Buffers = block I/O buffers; Cached = page cache for file reads; Shmem = tmpfs.

Reclaim pressure, not exhaustion, is the real signal: /proc/pressure/memory (some avg10=0.00 avg60=1.84 avg300=0.72 total=...) says what fraction of the time tasks were stalled waiting for memory. A growing avg60 matters even with plenty free.
MemoryHigh (soft, throttle and reclaim) versus MemoryMax (hard, OOM-kill) is the distinction to carry into 8.2.
commonMistakes: reading load average as a percentage of CPU; alerting on free memory instead of available or PSI; trusting %util on NVMe or RAID arrays; tuning tcp_fin_timeout down aggressively to "fix" TIME-WAIT (it breaks long-lived connections); treating CLOSE-WAIT as normal; running iostat once without an interval and drawing conclusions from the since-boot average; ignoring st on virtual machines and concluding the app is slow; using netstat instead of ss on a machine with tens of thousands of sockets; turning off swap "because Linux manages memory better" on a 512 MB VM.
practiceTasks: saturate a VM four ways (a busy loop, a memory hog, an fsync loop, and a fork bomb guarded by ulimit) and record uptime, free, vmstat 1 5, and iostat -x 1 for each, then write the diagnosis for each from those four commands alone. Then open 20 000 sockets to a dead port and drive CLOSE-WAIT to see the leak.

interviewQuestions.text: What exactly is the load average, and what does it count besides running processes?
Load average is 12 on a 4-CPU box and CPU idle is 70%. Where do you look, and what commands prove it?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Load 12 on 4 CPUs with 70% idle means the run queues are not full of CPU work, so the load number is counting something else. The most common cause is tasks in uninterruptible sleep, which the kernel includes in the load average because they are queued work that cannot proceed. So the first command is to look for D-state processes with ps -eo stat,pid,cmd | awk '$1 ~ /^D/', then iostat -xz 1 to see await and queue depth, and dmesg -T | tail for device errors or a hung NFS mount. The other possibility is thrashing, in which case vmstat 1 5 shows non-zero si and so columns, meaning processes are being pushed to swap and pulled back. A third possibility is that the run queue is full of tasks blocked on a lock rather than on CPU, which shows up as threads stuck in the same wait when you take a thread dump."

topics.title: Package management, patching, and hardening baselines
topics.description: keeping a host patched and configured consistently. The naive model is "log in and apt upgrade forever"; the mature model is that a host should be rebuildable, because long-lived hand-patched machines drift into states nobody can reproduce.
keyConcepts: Debian/Ubuntu (apt, dpkg)
apt update vs apt upgrade: update refreshes package *indexes*, upgrade installs. An upgrade without a recent update either does nothing or, worse, installs from stale metadata.
Read the simulation. A dist-upgrade that removes libssl1.1 or replaces openssh-server is a reboot-and-verify event, not a routine change.

/etc/apt/sources.list and /etc/apt/sources.list.d/*.list are the repository definition; .sources files (deb822 format) on newer releases. Add third-party repos with apt-key-free signing keys under /etc/apt/keyrings/ and signed-by=.
RHEL/Fedora/Rocky (dnf/yum)
dnf history undo is a real advantage of RPM-based systems and a genuine reason to prefer them on hosts you cannot easily rebuild.
dnf check-update exits 100 when updates exist, which trips naive CI wrappers.
Unattended security upgrades

Security patches fast (daily), regular patches on a planned cadence. A kernel or openssh-server patch means a reboot; schedule it and verify the service comes back (systemctl is-enabled, a smoke test, a boot-success check).
needrestart (or dnf-utils) tells you which services a library update would restart; the SSH daemon is the one you must never let restart carelessly.
Also patch the things apt does not know about: base images (8.2), language runtimes, language package trees (npm audit, pip-audit, cargo audit), and cloud-init/agent versions.
SSH key rotation, done properly
commonMistakes: running apt upgrade without apt update; applying a dist-upgrade on a Friday to a host you cannot reboot; holding a package "temporarily" for a year; putting secrets in a unit file or a .env in the image; treating a password change as offboarding; granting sudo ALL to a deploy account because "we needed it once"; automating reboots without a post-boot verification; ignoring base image and language-dependency patching because apt upgrade looked clean.
practiceTasks: build a hardening baseline script that verifies sshd settings, firewall state, service accounts, patch level, disk and log-retention config against a checklist and exits non-zero with a diff, run it against a stock VM, then rebuild the VM from a snapshot and re-run to show the drift disappears.

interviewQuestions.text: What is the difference between `apt update`, `apt upgrade`, `apt full-upgrade`, and `apt-get -s dist-upgrade`?
Why read the simulation before a `dist-upgrade`, and what kinds of packages make it risky?
What does `apt-mark hold` do, and when is it the right tool?
Which command finds which package owns a file on Debian vs RHEL?
What is a major advantage of `dnf history undo` over the Debian equivalent?
Configure unattended security upgrades. How do you test the configuration without applying it?
Why does an unattended kernel or `openssh-server` upgrade require care?
Give the correct four-step SSH key rotation procedure, and why is step 3 mandatory?
Why is removing an `authorized_keys` line the real offboarding step?
What is `expiry-time` in `authorized_keys`, and which OpenSSH version introduced it?
State the "rebuild, don't patch" principle in your own words and give one operational reason it reduces incident risk.
interviewQuestions.answer: "The point is that a long-lived host accumulates state that nobody wrote down: a hand-edited config, a package installed to make one thing work, a cron job added during an incident. After six months the host is a unique artifact, so 'works on prod' cannot be reproduced, you cannot reason about its risk, and every patch is a manual diff against a machine whose baseline you cannot state. Rebuilding from a versioned image plus configuration management makes the machine a function of its inputs, which means a bad change is reverted by replacing the instance, the previous state is reproducible, and drift shows up as a diff. It also moves patching from a maintenance window into image rebuilds, where the change is reviewed as code and rolled out to a fleet rather than host by host."

topics.title: Container networking
topics.description: Container networking within Containerization.
keyConcepts: Bridge networking (the default)

The default bridge network has no automatic DNS; container names are not resolvable (legacy --link was the workaround and is obsolete). Any user-defined bridge network gives you DNS for free through the embedded resolver at 127.0.0.11. This is the single most important networking fact: always create a user-defined network for multi-container apps.
Each network is a separate L2 segment with its own subnet; containers on different networks cannot talk by name or IP without routing through the host.
Port publishing vs a real port

-p does not open the container's port on the host. It adds a DNAT rule so traffic arriving at the host port is translated to the container's IP and port. The container's port is only reachable from inside its network namespace and from the host's published address.

Consequences: the container's port number and the host's port number are independent; you cannot publish two containers on the same host port; and the process inside still must listen on 0.0.0.0 (or the specific container IP) for publishing to work — an app bound to 127.0.0.1 inside a container is unreachable from outside, which is a common "why can't I reach it" answer.
host and none
Why localhost stops working across containers

Each container has its own network namespace, so 127.0.0.1 is a different loopback in each. localhost is a container-local address, not a service-discovery mechanism. Use the container/service name on a shared user-defined network.

Corollary for developers: localhost:5432 in a container is *that container's* Postgres (nonexistent), not the host's. Use the service name inside a Compose network, or host.docker.internal (Docker Desktop, or --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway on Linux).
DNS inside a container

The embedded DNS server forwards to the host's resolvers and answers container-name, network-alias, and network-name lookups from Docker's own records. It runs at 127.0.0.11:53 inside the container's netns.
commonMistakes: assuming EXPOSE publishes anything; relying on the default bridge's DNS; hardcoding container IPs; using localhost for a database URL inside a container; publishing to 0.0.0.0 when 127.0.0.1 suffices; --network host "just to debug" and shipping it; assuming the host firewall covers published ports (8.1.6); forgetting that two containers cannot share a published host port.
practiceTasks: build a two-container app (web + API) on a user-defined bridge, prove that name resolution works there and fails on the default bridge, show why localhost fails, add a --network-alias and resolve both names, then attach a third debug container with --network container:web and curl from inside the API's netns.

interviewQuestions.text: What is the embedded DNS server, which address does it listen on, and on which networks does it resolve names?
Why does `-p 8080:3000` not open the container's `3000`? What rule does Docker add?
Your app listens on `127.0.0.1:3000` inside a container and `curl` from the host fails with connection refused. Why, and what are two fixes?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Publishing forwards traffic arriving on the host's published address to the container's IP on the container's port, which only works if something inside the container is listening on a non-loopback address. An app bound to 127.0.0.1 is listening on the container's own loopback interface, and DNAT delivers the packet to the container's eth0 address, so nothing answers and the client gets a connection refusal. Two fixes: bind the app to 0.0.0.0 or to :: inside the container, which is the normal case, and if you want to keep loopback binding, put a reverse proxy in the same container or the same pod. It is the same class of bug as binding to 127.0.0.1 on a VM and wondering why the load balancer cannot reach it."

topics.title: Volumes
topics.description: Volumes within Containerization.
keyConcepts: Three kinds of mounts
The UID mismatch problem

A named volume is created empty, then populated from the image's contents at that path, preserving ownership. That is why /var/lib/postgresql/data ends up owned by uid 999 and works: the image's directory already belongs to the right user.
A bind mount of an empty host directory skips that step: the directory is created on the host owned by *you* (uid 1000), and every write as uid 1001 fails.
Fixes, in order of preference:
Use a named volume (ownership is inherited from the image).
Pre-create the host directory with the right owner: sudo chown -R 1001:1001 ./uploads or install -d -o 1001 -g 1001 ./uploads.
Pass --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" so the container uses your uid (great for dev bind mounts, bad for images that need a fixed uid like Postgres).
Use --mount type=bind with :Z (SELinux relabel) or :z (shared) on RHEL-family hosts, otherwise SELinux denies access even with correct DAC ownership.
A short entrypoint that fixes ownership then execs the real process — acceptable, but it must not be run on every restart of a large volume (a chown -R of a 100 GB volume on every boot is an outage).
Database data in volumes
Put pg_wal on its own volume so WAL writes are not interleaved with the bulk of the data on the same device; WAL on a slow or full volume is how a database stops accepting writes.
commonMistakes: -v with a relative path in a systemd unit or CI script (different cwd, different behaviour); bind-mounting over a directory the image needs; running as root "to fix" permissions inside a database container; docker compose down -v in a script against a production database; putting a large data set in a bind mount over NFS without thinking about file locking and latency; pruning volumes while a backup is running.
practiceTasks: start Postgres with a named volume, docker rm the container, restart it and prove the data survived; then switch to an empty bind mount and reproduce the UID failure, fix it with install -d -o 999 -g 999, and show df -h for a tmpfs /tmp versus a volume.

topics.title: Docker Compose
topics.description: a declarative file describing a multi-container application, plus a CLI that reconciles real containers against it. Compose is the standard local and single-host development-and-demos tool, and it is genuinely used for small internal deployments; it is not an orchestrator (8.3).
keyConcepts: depends_on health conditions — the semantics people get wrong

depends_on controls start *ordering*, not runtime availability. The database can still be down when your API connects, and Compose does not restart a service because its dependency became unhealthy. Your application must therefore handle "dependency not ready yet" at startup with retries and backoff; depends_on narrows the race, it does not remove it.
Prefer this for migrations:

The healthcheck's test must not depend on the tool being present. ["CMD", ...] does not use a shell, so no pipes or redirection; ["CMD-SHELL", ...] runs /bin/sh -c. curl -f http://localhost/ "works" until distroless has no shell or no curl.
Profiles: optional services and jobs
profiles: ["ops"] means the service only starts when --profile ops is given. Perfect for migrations, admin UIs, one-shot jobs, and debug sidecars that should not run in every environment.
Multiple profiles: --profile ops --profile debug. Services with no profile always start; services with any profile require that profile.
Compose auto-enables the test profile for a test directory in some versions; do not rely on that.
Interpolation and secrets in Compose

${VAR} comes from the shell environment or from a .env file next to compose.yaml; ${VAR:-default} supplies a default; ${VAR:?message} fails the whole command if the variable is unset, which is the right way to make a missing secret loud instead of silently connecting with an empty password.

env_file passes values to the container. It is not a secrets manager: the values live in a file on disk, show up in docker inspect, and end up in docker compose config output. For anything real, inject secrets at runtime from a manager (8.2.9) or mount a file.
docker compose config prints the fully interpolated config; treat its output as secret-bearing and never paste it into a bug report.
commonMistakes: assuming depends_on: [db] waits for the DB to be usable (it only waits for the container to start); restart: always on a job that should fail loudly; committing .env with real passwords; docker compose down -v in a runbook; version: keys left in the file (obsolete, and a warning in modern Compose); healthchecks using curl on distroless images; scaling without a load balancer so every replica takes 1/N of nothing useful.
practiceTasks: write the file above, run it, and prove depends_on semantics by breaking the database healthcheck and watching the API wait; then convert the API's startup into a retry loop and show it recovers without Compose restarting anything. Add an ops profile with a migration service and run it once with --profile ops run --rm.

interviewQuestions.text: What does `depends_on` actually guarantee, and what does it not?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Compose uses depends_on to order startup: with condition: service_healthy it will not start the dependent service until the dependency's healthcheck has passed. That is genuinely useful because it removes the most common race, an API booting before Postgres is accepting connections. What it does not do is manage runtime availability. Compose has no idea the database went away, it will not restart the API when that happens, and the healthcheck only runs while a container is starting, so a dependency that becomes unhealthy after startup is invisible to Compose. So the honest design is: use depends_on with a health condition to reduce the startup race, and still give the application retry-with-backoff on startup, plus real reconnection logic at runtime. If you need the dependency relationship to be enforced continuously, that is an orchestrator's job, not a Compose job."

interviewQuestions.text: Compare `service_started`, `service_healthy`, and `service_completed_successfully`. When is each right?

topics.title: Security scanning
topics.description: The controls required because a single endpoint now executes arbitrary selection over a whole graph: per-field authorization, query cost limits, introspection policy, batching limits, and depth limits.
keyConcepts: Query depth and complexity

Depth blocks the recursive pattern (parent { parent { parent ... } }) and cycle exploitation. A max depth of 7-10 for internal apps, 5-6 for public ones. It is cheap, and it catches the obvious abuse.
Complexity is what actually costs you; measure list sizes, not field counts (5.5.3). A static estimator with per-field multipliers plus a per-operation budget is the practical answer.
Timeout: a hard server-side query deadline (AbortSignal or a driver statement timeout) so a query that slipped under the cost budget still cannot run forever.

Also cap: aliases per query, fragment count, introspection depth, the number of variables, and the total request body size. Alias-batching is the most under-appreciated vector — 10,000 aliases of one field is 10,000 units of work in one HTTP request.
Disable introspection in production
Persisted queries / allowlists
Automatic (APQ) — clients may register new queries at runtime. Convenient; still lets an attacker run *any* query your type system allows, subject to depth/complexity limits.

Allowlist — only pre-registered hashes are served. This is genuinely strong: the endpoint becomes a fixed set of operations. It does mean a client with a dynamically-built query needs a registration step, and every client update requires re-registration, so it suits first-party clients and published APIs with managed consumers.
Field-level allowlists per role (a "whitelist graph" of what each role may query) are powerful and brittle; treat them as defence in depth, not the primary control.
Field-level authorization

Defense in depth, in order: database row-level security (or a mandatory tenant predicate in the repository) is the backstop; a directive or a resolver check is the readable layer; a gateway-level field allowlist is the outer layer. Any one of them can be forgotten.
commonMistakes: a per-row authorization query in a field resolver; hoisting one check for the whole list; trusting @skip for access control; believing introspection-off is a security control; no first cap; allowing HTTP batching of operations without per-operation cost limits; interpolating variables into SQL inside a resolver; a GET query in a cookie-authenticated API without CSRF protection.
practiceTasks: add depth and complexity limits, disable introspection, and enable both APQ and allowlist modes (switchable by env) to a GraphQL API. Then attempt, in a test suite: a depth-20 recursive query, a 1,000-alias query, a first: 1000000 query, an orders { canEdit } query on 1,000 rows (count queries before and after batching), an un-registered query under allowlist, a query with a variable from another tenant, and a GET query without a CSRF token.

interviewQuestions.text: Why is a field count a bad complexity measure?
Does `introspection: false` actually secure the API?
What is the N+1 authz trap, and what is the tempting-but-wrong fix?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a GraphQL API where the team added a canEdit field to Order so the UI could hide an Edit button, and each check was a per-row permissions query. Decision: two changes — batch the check with a DataLoader so it is one query per request, and, more importantly, express the permission as a row filter in SQL rather than a post-filter, so unauthorized orders never leave the database. Reasoning: a per-row authorization check is a database query inside a field resolver, which is the N+1 pattern wearing a security costume. With first: 100 it is 101 queries, and the endpoint is slow for large pages while looking fine in development with five orders. The tempting fix, and the one I have seen in production code reviews, is to hoist the check: fetch the permission once for the current user, then return that single value for every order in the list. That is a data-leak vulnerability, not an optimization — the user is authorized to view *some* orders, so the list is authorized, and now the field reports the same capability for orders they must not touch. The UI would show an Edit button on an order they cannot edit, and any client could act on it. So the rule is: authorization must be evaluated per object, and the cheap way to evaluate it per object is batching, not memoizing. Trade-offs: batching a permission check needs the key to be the object and the value to be a boolean, so you need a well-indexed permissions(order_id, principal_id) table and a query that returns exactly one row per requested id — if the table is missing rows, "absent" must mean "denied", which is an easy thing to get backwards. Failure scenario: a team batches the check correctly, then later optimizes the query with SELECT order_id, bool_or(...) and forgets the tenant_id predicate, so ids from another tenant resolve to false and users see orders they should not see at all — a batching optimization that quietly became a tenant boundary."

topics.title: What a container is
topics.description: What a container is within Containerization.
keyConcepts: Namespaces: the isolation primitives

Mount namespace + overlayfs is what gives a container its filesystem view. chroot gives you a directory; namespaces plus pivot_root give you a coherent view of /, /proc, /dev, and /sys that changes when the container starts.
net namespace explains the most common beginner confusion: inside a container, 127.0.0.1 is *that container's* loopback. Two containers sharing localhost are two different machines.
user namespaces map container UIDs to host UIDs, which is what makes rootless Docker possible: your unprivileged UID becomes root inside the container with no privileges on the host.
Cgroups: the limits

cgroups do not provide namespacing; they provide accounting and limits for CPU time, memory, PIDs, disk I/O bandwidth and IO weight. Namespaces provide visibility isolation; cgroups provide resource control. Together they are what "container" means to the kernel.
systemd puts every unit and every user session in its own cgroup, which is why systemd-cgtop and systemctl show -p MemoryCurrent work.
Overlay filesystems: the writable layer
Reads walk lowerdir from top to bottom. The first write copies up the file into upperdir (copy-on-write), which is why a container can make a read-only image file writable.
Deleting a lower-layer file creates a whiteout character device (major 0, minor 0) in the upper layer. It does not free the original blocks.

Consequences that explain most container disk puzzles: rm inside a container does not shrink the image; the upper layer grows for the life of the container; renaming or hard-linking a file that lives in a lower layer fails or triggers copy-up; and docker commit of a container bakes its upper layer into an image.
Container vs VM
commonMistakes: calling a container a VM in an interview (it is the single most common tell); assuming --privileged containers are still just containers; expecting rm in a container to free host disk; writing to the image layer in a long-running container and then wondering why the disk is full; assuming you can use a host firewall's input rules to filter container traffic (Docker bypasses them, 8.1.6); forgetting that a container cannot see host processes without --pid=host; assuming docker run of any public image is safe.
practiceTasks: run alpine and ubuntu and diff /proc/self/mountinfo, ip addr, and ps output; start a busy process in a container and find it on the host; write a 50 MB file inside a container, delete it, and show the host's disk usage is unchanged; then run the same app in a container with --pid=host --network=host and note which isolations disappeared.

interviewQuestions.text: Name the Linux namespaces and what each one isolates.
What does the `pid` namespace do to signal handling and zombie reaping, and why does that matter for containers?
What is the difference between the mount namespace and a chroot?
What problem do cgroups solve that namespaces do not?
Explain overlayfs: `lowerdir`, `upperdir`, `merged`, `workdir`, and what a whiteout entry is.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Overlayfs presents one directory that is a stack of directories. lowerdir is the read-only chain of image layers, read from the top down so later layers shadow earlier ones. upperdir is the container's writable layer, and merged is the union the container actually sees as its root. The first write to a file that lives in lowerdir is a copy-up: the file is copied into upperdir and only then modified, which is what makes read-only image files writable without touching the image. Deleting a lower file does not delete it; overlayfs writes a whiteout entry, a character device with device 0:0, into upperdir. That is the key consequence: whiteouts and copies consume space in upperdir, so removing files inside a long-running container shrinks nothing, and the disk keeps growing until the container is removed."

interviewQuestions.text: Why does `rm` inside a container not free space on the host's disk?
What is copy-up, and which operations surprise people because of it?
Fill in the container-vs-VM table for boot time, isolation, density, and attack surface. Which one would you use for a kernel driver?
A colleague says "a container is a lightweight VM". What is wrong with that, practically?
interviewQuestions.answer: "A container shares the host kernel, so a container is exactly as trustworthy as the kernel it runs on, and the attack surface is the syscall interface rather than a hypervisor boundary. Practically, it breaks in three ways. First, expectations: people assume an isolation boundary comparable to a VM and expose a container that has not been hardened. Second, portability: 'any image anywhere' is false, because it has to be Linux with a compatible kernel, and a kernel version you need may not be available on the host. Third, operations: you cannot expect a different OS, a different kernel, or hardware passthrough, and you should not expect kernel CVEs to be irrelevant. What containers are is a packaging and deployment mechanism that happens to include some isolation, and the right way to think about it is that the isolation is one of several layers, with immutable images, minimal privileges, no secrets in the image, and blast-radius limits doing the rest of the work."

topics.title: Images and layers
topics.description: Images and layers within Containerization.
keyConcepts: Anatomy

Layers are content-addressed by digest (sha256:...), so identical layers across images are stored and transferred once. A manifest points at a config plus a layer list; the config records Env, Cmd, Entrypoint, User, WorkingDir, ExposedPorts, Volumes, Labels, and creation timestamps.
Layer caching: the rule and the consequence
Each instruction that changes the filesystem produces a layer. The build cache key is the instruction plus the digests of the layers before it (plus, for ADD/COPY, a checksum of the source files).
Order instructions from least to most frequently changing. Copying the lockfile first means dependency installation is a cache hit on every source-only change.
Anything that invalidates a cache from above: changing FROM, a build ARG used in an earlier RUN, ADD/COPY of a directory whose contents changed, ENV/ARG values that appear before, and --no-cache.

The legacy builder computed cache keys less precisely; BuildKit (the default in modern Docker) uses content-based checksums and mount options like RUN --mount=type=cache. --progress=plain makes its output readable in CI.
Layer bloat, and squashing with multi-stage builds
Every file written in a RUN belongs to that layer forever, even if a later RUN deletes it. Deleting in the same layer avoids it; deleting in a later layer only adds a whiteout.

The standard offenders: apt-get update + apt-get install without rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* in the *same* layer, npm install (cache in /root/.npm), pip install (cache in /root/.cache/pip), downloaded tarballs left behind, build tools left in the runtime image.
Multi-stage builds are the fix and are now the default expectation: the builder stage keeps the toolchain, the runtime stage copies only artifacts.
docker buildx build --output type=oci plus a tool like syft/docker-slim can also shrink an image, and distroless or Alpine base images avoid the problem (8.2.9).
commonMistakes: COPY . . before npm ci and wondering why CI takes eleven minutes; apt-get install without cleaning the lists in the same layer; treating docker commit as a deploy method; pulling latest in a deploy pipeline; assuming docker rmi freed host disk when a container still holds the layers; copying node_modules from the build host into the image (wrong arch, wrong libc, giant layer); publishing intermediate build stages to a public registry.
practiceTasks: build a single-stage image with a bloated apt layer and measure it with docker history, convert it to a multi-stage build, measure again, then flip the COPY order to break and restore the cache, timing both builds with time docker build and --progress=plain.

interviewQuestions.text: What are the parts of an image on disk and in a registry, and how are they addressed?
Why does copying `package.json` before the source matter so much for build speed?
Give a Dockerfile where every source change busts the dependency cache. Then fix the order.
`RUN apt-get install ...` then `RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` in a later layer: did that shrink anything? Why?
interviewQuestions.answer: "No. Deleting the apt list in a later layer only writes a whiteout into a new layer; the original package index bytes remain in the earlier layer, and a registry or a host that stores layers by digest still keeps them. The size of an image is the sum of its layers, so the space is not recovered. The fix is either to do the install and the cleanup in the same RUN, so the layer never contains the lists, or, better, to put everything into a build stage that is not part of the final image at all, which is what a multi-stage build is for. The general lesson is that you cannot shrink a layer after the fact; shrinking happens at the instruction, not at the delete."

topics.title: Dockerfile instructions
topics.description: Dockerfile instructions within Containerization.
keyConcepts: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT, and shell form vs exec form

Rule: exec form everywhere, ENTRYPOINT for the fixed binary, CMD for the overridable arguments. If you need a shell to combine commands, make sure it execs: CMD ["/bin/sh", "-c", "exec node dist/server.js"].
If an image must be usable both as a tool and a service: ENTRYPOINT the tool, and let CMD be overridden.
dumb-init, tini, or --init solves PID-1 zombie reaping and signal forwarding robustly, at ~1 MB of image size.
ENV vs ARG

ARG values are available during build only, and are recorded in build metadata and often visible in docker history --no-trunc if you use them in a layer. ARG NPM_TOKEN followed by RUN echo $NPM_TOKEN is a leak.
ENV values live permanently in the image config and are printed by docker inspect, docker history, and any docker save. Never a secret.
Use BuildKit secret mounts for build-time secrets:
Runtime secrets come from the platform (8.2.9), not the image.
HEALTHCHECK semantics

Semantics: run --interval apart; a run is healthy on exit 0, unhealthy otherwise; after --retries consecutive failures the container is unhealthy; failures during --start-period do not count (and --start-interval allows faster checks during startup).

The status is recorded in .State.Health and visible in docker ps. Kubernetes ignores Docker's healthcheck and uses livenessProbe/readinessProbe/startupProbe (8.3), so define both: the in-image check for local and single-host use, the probes for orchestration.
commonMistakes: shell-form CMD with a Node server and a 10-second docker stop timeout; ARG NPM_TOKEN in a Dockerfile; ENV DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@db in an image; EXPOSE believing it publishes; a VOLUME for something that must persist but using an anonymous volume; running as root because USER broke a write to /app; ADD a URL during build; HEALTHCHECK that only proves the process exists rather than that the service works; relying on Docker's healthcheck in Kubernetes.
practiceTasks: build a tiny Node image with exec-form and shell-form ENTRYPOINT, start both with docker run -d, and show that docker stop on the shell-form one takes the full timeout and logs no shutdown message while the exec-form one shuts down gracefully; then add --init, dumb-init, and a HEALTHCHECK that hits a real endpoint and prove docker ps reports unhealthy when you break the endpoint.

interviewQuestions.text: What is the difference between `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT`, and how do they combine when you pass arguments to `docker run`?
Why is shell form harmful for `ENTRYPOINT`/`CMD`? Explain what happens to `docker stop`.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Shell form runs the command through /bin/sh -c, so the shell becomes PID 1 and your binary is its child. Two things break. First, signals: PID 1 in a container does not get the kernel's default signal dispositions, so SIGTERM from docker stop is delivered to the shell, and sh only forwards it to its child in some situations and some shells; the practical result is that the shutdown handler never runs, the container waits out the 10-second stop timeout, and Docker escalates to SIGKILL, which means no graceful drain, no buffer flush, and killed in-flight requests. Second, zombies: PID 1 is responsible for reaping orphans, and a shell does not do that well. Exec form, CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"], makes the binary PID 1 so it receives signals directly, and if you still need a shell for something, exec node dist/server.js inside it, or use dumb-init/tini via --init."

topics.title: A production multi-stage Dockerfile
topics.description: A production multi-stage Dockerfile within Containerization.
keyConcepts: The target
Why each line exists
Demonstrating the cache
Reproducibility

Pin the base by digest, use npm ci with a committed lockfile, pin tool versions (npx tsc@5.6.3 or a devDependencies lock), avoid latest anywhere in a tag chain, avoid RUN curl ... | bash, and set SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH if you care about timestamp reproducibility.
Record provenance: --provenance=true --sbom=true with docker buildx attaches an SBOM and a signed provenance statement to the pushed image (8.2.10).
Reproducible does not mean identical across architectures unless you build for each and select by digest.
commonMistakes: committing the Dockerfile without .dockerignore; npm install in CI instead of npm ci; leaving dev dependencies in the runtime stage "just in case"; running as root because the app needs to write to /app (fix ownership instead); no USER at all so the container can read /proc/1/environ of other containers' neighbours on the same host; ARG secrets; EXPOSE mistaken for publishing; no STOPSIGNAL/ENTRYPOINT handling so docker stop always needs SIGKILL.
practiceTasks: build this exact Dockerfile for a real project, prove the cache behaviour by touching a source file and then reordering COPY layers with timings, compare the single-stage and multi-stage image sizes with docker history, run it as uid 1001 with --read-only plus a tmpfs, and confirm that docker stop finishes in under a second with a "draining" log line.

interviewQuestions.text: Why is this Dockerfile four stages instead of one, and what specifically leaks into the image without them?
What does `--mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm` change, and why is that different from caching `node_modules` in a layer?

Why does `npm prune --omit=dev` matter for security and not just size?

Why numeric `USER 1001:1001` instead of `USER node`?
What does `dumb-init` actually do that the Node process cannot do as PID 1?
interviewQuestions.answer: "There are two things a PID 1 must do that an ordinary process may not. It must reap orphaned children, because PID 1 is the reaper for the entire process tree once their parents are gone, and Node does not install a SIGCHLD handler that calls wait on every child, so short-lived processes that fork and exit become zombies that accumulate until the PID table fills. And it must handle signals explicitly, because the kernel does not apply default dispositions to PID 1: SIGTERM only reaches the Node process because Node installs its own handler, but any child process started by the app, and any signal the app does not handle, will simply never be delivered. dumb-init is about 1 MB, installs handlers for the full signal set, forwards signals to the whole process group, and reaps zombies, which makes the container behave like a normally launched process on a host."

topics.title: Volumes and storage
topics.description: Volumes and storage within Containerization.
keyConcepts: Three kinds of mounts
The UID mismatch problem

A named volume is created empty, then populated from the image's contents at that path, preserving ownership. That is why /var/lib/postgresql/data ends up owned by uid 999 and works: the image's directory already belongs to the right user.
A bind mount of an empty host directory skips that step: the directory is created on the host owned by *you* (uid 1000), and every write as uid 1001 fails.
Fixes, in order of preference:
Use a named volume (ownership is inherited from the image).
Pre-create the host directory with the right owner: sudo chown -R 1001:1001 ./uploads or install -d -o 1001 -g 1001 ./uploads.
Pass --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" so the container uses your uid (great for dev bind mounts, bad for images that need a fixed uid like Postgres).
Use --mount type=bind with :Z (SELinux relabel) or :z (shared) on RHEL-family hosts, otherwise SELinux denies access even with correct DAC ownership.
A short entrypoint that fixes ownership then execs the real process — acceptable, but it must not be run on every restart of a large volume (a chown -R of a 100 GB volume on every boot is an outage).
Database data in volumes
Put pg_wal on its own volume so WAL writes are not interleaved with the bulk of the data on the same device; WAL on a slow or full volume is how a database stops accepting writes.
commonMistakes: -v with a relative path in a systemd unit or CI script (different cwd, different behaviour); bind-mounting over a directory the image needs; running as root "to fix" permissions inside a database container; docker compose down -v in a script against a production database; putting a large data set in a bind mount over NFS without thinking about file locking and latency; pruning volumes while a backup is running.
practiceTasks: start Postgres with a named volume, docker rm the container, restart it and prove the data survived; then switch to an empty bind mount and reproduce the UID failure, fix it with install -d -o 999 -g 999, and show df -h for a tmpfs /tmp versus a volume.

topics.title: Resource limits and health
topics.description: Resource limits and health within Containerization.
keyConcepts: Why limits are not optional

Unbounded containers are the classic noisy-neighbour failure: one leak in one service gets the process OOM-killed by the kernel, or the CPU saturated by one runaway loop, and every other container on the host feels it.
Limits are also the *language* an orchestrator uses to schedule: requests drive placement, limits drive eviction order under pressure (Kubernetes 8.3).

--memory interacts with V8. If the cgroup allows 512 MB and Node's default heap ceiling is ~2 GB, the kernel kills the process before V8 feels pressure, with no GC pressure and no error message. Set NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=440 (about 85% of the limit) so the GC reacts first. Same idea for the JVM (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75), Python (PYTHONMALLOC/gc tuning), Redis (maxmemory), and Postgres (work_mem times max_connections).
Observing limits in action
nr_throttled close to nr_periods means your --cpus quota is starving the process: latency rises while CPU usage looks "only" at the limit.
OOM kill in a container
Exit code 137 = 128 + 9 = SIGKILL, and OOMKilled: true tells you it was the memory limit, not a crash and not your code calling process.exit.
With restart: always, you get a crash loop. The signal is OOMKilled plus a rising oom_kill counter in memory.events, not the logs.
Health and restart semantics
Docker's restart backoff doubles from 100 ms and caps at about a minute; there is no built-in rate limiter equivalent to systemd's StartLimitBurst, so a crash loop can spam the host.
--restart and --stop-timeout and --health-* are all daemon-level docker run flags; in Compose they are the restart, stop_grace_period, and healthcheck keys.
commonMistakes: setting --memory equal to or above the host's memory (a container can then take the whole machine); no --pids-limit; --ulimit nofile left at the 1024 default so a busy Node app dies with EMFILE under load; restart: always on a job that exits 0 successfully; docker stats used as an alert source with no memory limit set anywhere; a healthcheck that only checks the process is alive, so an app wedged on a dead database still reports healthy.
practiceTasks: run a container with --memory=128m and no --max-old-space-size, watch it get OOM-killed, then set the heap limit to ~85% and watch the GC kick in instead; add --cpus=0.25 and read cpu.stat to prove throttling; set --pids-limit=16 and try to fork 100 children; then verify docker update can change limits on a live container.

interviewQuestions.text: What does `--memory=512m` map to, and what happens at exactly that number?
Why set `--memory-swap` equal to `--memory`, and what does that mean for the container?
`--cpus=1.5` versus `--cpu-shares=512`: what is the difference in behaviour when the host is busy?
What causes `Cannot fork: Resource temporarily unavailable`, and which flag fixes it?
Your Node container is killed with exit 137 and no stack trace. Diagnose it in three commands and one fix.
interviewQuestions.answer: "First, docker inspect --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' api: OOMKilled: true with exit code 137 (128 plus SIGKILL) means the kernel killed the process because the cgroup's memory limit was exceeded, and it was not my code calling process.exit and not a segfault, which would be 139. Second, docker exec api cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.events to confirm oom_kill is incrementing, and docker logs --tail 20 to see whether the app printed anything before dying; a Node app with no output at all plus OOMKilled: true is the classic signature, because SIGKILL runs no handler. The fix is twofold: give the process headroom so it GCs before the limit hits, by setting NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size to roughly 80-85% of the container limit, and find the actual leak with a heap snapshot, because raising the limit only moves the cliff."

topics.title: Container security
topics.description: Container security within Containerization.
keyConcepts: The threat model in one paragraph
Rootless mode

Rootless Docker runs dockerd as your unprivileged user, uses a user namespace so container root maps to a non-root host uid, and uses slirp4netns or RootlessKit for networking. Consequences: a container escape lands as your user rather than as host root; no privileged containers or --net=host; uid mapping means files created in bind mounts are owned by *you* on the host.

Limits: no host networking, no --privileged, limited cgroup delegation (--cgroupns=host requires delegation), slightly more networking overhead. Available on Linux with kernel 4.18+ or 5.4+ for cgroup v2.
Running as non-root
Numeric UIDs mean no /etc/passwd entry is needed, which is required for distroless images and for Kubernetes runAsNonRoot.

A container that runs as non-root on the host's user namespace mapping can still be root inside its namespace, so "non-root in the container" is about host-mapping, not magic. Use rootless mode or userns-remap to make that true.
Bind mounts with --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" give you correct local file ownership while developing.
Hardening flags, all real

Capabilities are the fine-grained version of root: CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE (bind port <1024), CAP_NET_RAW (ping, packet sniffing), CAP_SYS_ADMIN (mount, most of the scary stuff). Docker's default set is ~14 capabilities; dropping all and adding back one is the pattern.

seccomp is a syscall allowlist enforced by the kernel in BPF. The default Docker profile exists because the syscall surface is enormous and most workloads use a small fraction of it. A custom profile is JSON:
Read-only root filesystem is one of the highest-value hardening options and is nearly free: --read-only plus --tmpfs /tmp plus explicit volumes for the two or three directories the app writes.
commonMistakes: --privileged in a Compose file because "the app needs it"; ENV with a DATABASE_URL containing a password; no .dockerignore; leaving dev dependencies in a production image so an app vulnerability has more surface; trusting latest; scanning only at build time; giving a container SYS_ADMIN "temporarily"; logging tokens and full request headers; running the production image on node:22 (full) instead of slim or distroless; treating a container's non-root user as equivalent to rootless mode.
practiceTasks: take a public image, pull the secret out of a layer with docker save + tar, then rebuild the image correctly (secret injected at runtime from a file, .dockerignore in place, npm ci --omit=dev, numeric USER, cap-drop ALL, --read-only) and prove with trivy image and docker history that the leak is gone; then run it with --read-only plus a tmpfs and confirm the app still starts.

interviewQuestions.text: What is rootless Docker, what does it protect you from, and what can you not do with it?
Why run as a non-root user, and why a *numeric* uid?
What does `--read-only` break, and what do you add back?
What are Linux capabilities, and why `cap-drop ALL`?
What is seccomp, what does the default profile block, and what is `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` for?
What is `no-new-privileges` and which escalation class does it stop?
Why is `--privileged` effectively equivalent to root on the host?
Explain, step by step, how a secret ends up inside an image via `ENV`, via `ARG`, and via `COPY . .`.
Show how to find a `.env` inside a published image's layers, and why removing it from the repo afterwards does not help.
interviewQuestions.answer: "The mechanism is that an image is a sequence of immutable, content-addressed layer tarballs plus a config JSON, and the config records every ENV. So first I docker save the image, which produces an archive of blobs/sha256/<digest> layer tars plus manifest.json. I read the config digest out of manifest.json, extract that JSON, and print Config.Env, which gives you any ENV value directly, including a secret one. For anything copied in with COPY, I loop over the layer tarballs with tar -tf looking for .env and then tar -xOf the matching path to print its contents, which finds the file in whichever layer introduced it. crane export and skopeo do the same thing without a daemon. The point of the exercise is that the answer is knowable by anyone who can pull, and removing the file from source afterwards changes nothing: the old digest still exists and the registry still serves it until garbage collection, and the credential has to be rotated regardless."

interviewQuestions.text: What must you do after a secret has been in a published image?
When would you use a BuildKit secret mount instead of an `ARG`?
Why is a Docker `HEALTHCHECK` not a security control?

keyConcepts: Accessibility (a11y)

Automated scanning (axe-core, Lighthouse, Pa11y, eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y): catches roughly 20-40% of issues -- missing labels, contrast, missing alt, invalid ARIA, heading order, duplicate ids, focus order in simple cases.

Manual expert testing (keyboard, screen reader, zoom, forced colors, motion): catches the rest -- the ones a machine cannot judge (alt text *quality*, focus *visibility*, reading order *sense*, error message *clarity*, timeout sufficiency).
User testing with disabled people: catches what neither of the first two can -- whether the experience is actually usable and non-embarrassing.
The legal and commercial frame you need to know for interviews

Keyboard only. Unplug the mouse. Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Escape, arrow keys. Every interactive element reachable, in a sensible order, with a visible focus indicator at every stop. No keyboard traps. Skip links work.

Screen reader (NVDA on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS/iOS, Orca on Linux). Learn the basics of one properly. Test: every image's alt text is *meaningful* (not "image1.jpg"); every form field has a label; errors are announced and associated; dynamic content is announced via a live region; the page has one h1 and a sane heading structure; tables have headers; the document language is set; landmarks (header, nav, main, footer) exist.
Zoom and reflow. 200% browser zoom, and 400% on a 1280px viewport (WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow). No horizontal scrolling, no clipped content, no overlapping text.

Colour and contrast. Text contrast >= 4.5:1 (normal) and 3:1 (large, >= 24px or 19px bold). Non-text contrast >= 3:1 for UI components and focus indicators. Never colour alone to convey meaning. Check with a simulator for deuteranopia/protanopia/tritanopia and for achromatopsia.
Forced colours / high contrast mode (Windows High Contrast, prefers-contrast: more). Your custom colours often disappear.
Reduced motion. prefers-reduced-motion: reduce honoured: no parallax, no auto-playing carousels, no large transitions. prefers-reduced-transparency, prefers-contrast, forced-colors.
Text spacing (WCAG 1.4.12): with the bookmarklet applying 1.5x line-height, 1.5x letter-spacing, 4px word-spacing, 1.2x paragraph-spacing, nothing clips.
commonMistakes: an accessibility statement that claims conformance with a level you have not audited; automated checks run only pre-release; no issue tracking or SLA for a11y bugs; and treating WCAG as a checklist rather than as an outcome measured with disabled users.
