topics.title: Feature flags
topics.description: A remote configuration mechanism that lets you change runtime behaviour without shipping code. Cross-reference PHASE 8 → CI/CD → feature flags for the delivery side; here is the frontend correctness side.
keyConcepts: Types of flag, with the frontend consequence
Targeting rules
User id (stable, precise, but only usable after login — so pre-login experiences need something else).
Tenant/organisation (the usual choice for B2B: one rollout decision per customer).
Cohort/attribute (country, plan, app version, device class) — needs a stable bucketing hash of a *stable* attribute; changing the attribute reassigns users and destroys your experiment data.
Percentage (0–100%) via a deterministic hash of a stable id (user id, or anonymous id before login), not Math.random():
Gradual rollout: ramp 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%, advancing on an SLO/metric gate rather than on a date.
Exposure events and experiment analysis
Emit exposure once per (flag, variant, user/session) with a stable id, and only when the variant was actually rendered.

Gate analysis on exposure, not assignment. Filtering on assignment dilutes results with users who never reached the UI — usually a large and *biased* fraction (they may have bounced early or errored).
Sticky assignment plus a shared id across devices is what makes results trustworthy; without it, users flip variants between sessions and your metrics become noise.
Flag lifecycle (the part teams skip)
commonMistakes: using Math.random() for bucketing; logging assignment and calling it exposure; no owner or expiry; baking flag values into build-time env; caching HTML without the variant in the key; assuming client flags are trustworthy for access control; leaving 100%-rolled-out flags forever.
practiceTasks: implement a flag SDK over a static JSON config with deterministic hash bucketing, an useFlag hook, an exposure logger with dedupe, and typed definitions including owner/expires. Then write a CI script that fails on expired flags and prints a report of flags by age and usage, and reproduce the hydration-mismatch bug by evaluating a flag differently on server and client — then fix it.

interviewQuestions.text: What kinds of feature flags exist, and which ones should never expire?
How should percentage rollouts be bucketed so assignment is sticky and independent?
Where should a flag be evaluated, and what goes wrong if you evaluate on the wrong side?
Explain assignment vs exposure and why analysis must gate on exposure.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: experiment analysis has to attribute an outcome to the variant a user actually saw. Decision: emit one exposure event per flag, variant, and user id at the moment the variant is rendered, and define the analysis population as users with an exposure event, not users with an assignment event. Reasoning: assignment happens at evaluation time — which might be at app boot, on a route the user never visits, on a payload the client discards, or in a code path that throws before render. Users in the assigned-but-unexposed group are systematically different from exposed users: they are the ones who bounced early, hit an error, or never reached the UI at all. Including them biases the experiment toward whatever the unexposed population does, and it dilutes effect size toward zero, so you can easily fail to detect a real win. Exposure also gives the denominator you actually need for funnel conversion. Trade-offs: exposure logging is extra client work and needs dedupe by (flag, variant, user) so page navigation does not inflate counts; it also means you must handle a variant that renders conditionally inside an error boundary, where an exposure may be logged for something the user did not perceive. Failure scenario: we ship a pricing-layout experiment, assign 50/50, log assignment at boot, and read a 2% conversion lift as real — but exposure logging shows only 20% of assigned users ever reached the pricing table, and the lift was entirely inside the wrong population; the team ships a change that does nothing. Alternative: define exposure at a well-chosen semantic point (the component that actually differs) rather than at the flag read, and validate the exposure rate per arm as a sanity check — an exposure rate near zero or near 100% means the measurement point is wrong."

topics.title: Nginx (reverse proxy, load balancing, SSL termination)
topics.description: A Proxy is a stand-in for another object that intercepts operations on it. In design-pattern terms it is the structural version of Decorator: instead of hand-forwarding each method, you intercept property access generically. JavaScript ships this as a language feature, so "the Proxy pattern" and "the JS Proxy API" are the same conversation.
keyConcepts: Difficulty
Real uses, in rough order of production value
Boundary validation and normalisation. A Proxy in front of parsed external input converts "trust the payload" into "validate the payload", without you writing a DTO per field.
Lazy initialisation / virtual fields. A Proxy that materialises a field from a loader on first access removes the if (!this.x) this.x = load() pattern from constructors.

Memoisation. Intercept get, look up a WeakMap cache, compute on miss. Careful: the cache key must be the *receiver*, not the proxy, or you get infinite recursion. And you must not memoise anything with a side effect.
Read-only views. A Proxy that throws on set/delete/defineProperty makes immutability real rather than readonly-by-convention (readonly in TypeScript compiles away; Object.freeze is shallow).
Deprecation shims and API migration. Wrap a legacy module and log which old methods are still called — you get migration telemetry for free, and the shim disappears when the log goes quiet.
ORM/SDK property-access translation — a snake_case API exposed as camelCase.
Tracing instrumentation — the logged decorator from 11.1.6.
Use when the interception is *generic* (applies to all properties) or *derived from data* (a spec-driven validator), or when the value is genuinely lazy and expensive.
Use in dev/test code: a debug Proxy that logs unexpected property reads is a fantastic way to find which properties of a mock a test actually depends on.
Don't use on hot paths: every property access becomes a trap with megamorphic dispatch; a Proxy-heavy inner loop can be several times slower than the plain version, and it defeats inline caches.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain difficulty and when you would use it.
Explain real uses, in rough order of production value and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: You gain: one place for a whole class of concerns, zero per-field code, composability. You pay: (a) readability — a reader sees p.foo and cannot know a trap runs; (b) debuggability — the stack shows the proxy, not the target; (c) invariants — you can throw TypeError from a proxy that violates an invariant, which is the worst class of bug; (d) performance on hot paths; (e) typeof, instanceof, and identity subtleties that surprise people (p instanceof Foo works; p.constructor returns your trapped value if you trap it wrong).

topics.title: Object storage
topics.description: Object storage within Cloud Platforms.
keyConcepts: Multipart upload: CreateMultipartUpload → UploadPart (each part at least 5MB except the last, at most 10,000 parts, so the maximum object is about 5TB) → CompleteMultipartUpload. Benefits: resumable uploads of large files, parallel throughput, and per-part retry. Costs: you must clean up aborted uploads, and each part is a separate object until completion. Abandoned multipart uploads are billed forever — an AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle rule is the single most valuable line in an S3 lifecycle configuration.

ETag semantics: for a single-part upload the ETag is the MD5 of the content; for a multipart upload it is a hash of the part hashes, so it is not the MD5 and cannot be used for integrity verification. Use ChecksumAlgorithm (SHA-256) per part and per object if you need real verification, and verify on the download path.

Presigned URLs: a signed URL grants time-limited access to a specific key and method, which is how you upload directly from a browser without proxying bytes through your app. Critical details: the expiry (as short as possible, minutes for uploads), the Content-Type is part of the signature if you sign it, the URL is a bearer credential (anyone with it has access until expiry), and you must constrain the key prefix per user (PUT only under uploads/<userId>/) because a client that can choose any key can overwrite anything. Never sign a prefix wildcard.

Eventual consistency, carefully: PUT/GET of a single object is strongly read-after-write consistent in current S3. What is eventually consistent is: LIST (directory listings) and HEAD for an object that was just deleted or overwritten concurrently, CopyObject and DELETE interactions, and the replication to a secondary region (which is eventually consistent and is a documented design assumption). For strong consistency on listing behaviour, there is a consistent-read option in newer object stores; if you need a list-and-read invariant, design around it (a manifest object, or a database as the index).

No rename and no partial update. Renaming is CopyObject + Delete, which for a large object is a full server-side copy (billed) and is not atomic. Any "edit" of an object is a full new object. This is why object storage plus a pointer in a database is the pattern for "immutable objects, mutable references": the object is written once, and the row that points at it is updated in a transaction, and the old version is deleted later.

Versioning gives you rollback, and it interacts badly with cost: every delete becomes a marker, storage grows, and you must add lifecycle rules to expire non-current versions. Versioning is what makes accidental deletion recoverable, and it is worth enabling on anything you cannot regenerate.

Lifecycle rules are the cost control: expire by age, transition to infrequent-access or archive storage classes by age, abort incomplete multipart uploads after N days, and expire previous versions after N days. Archive storage classes have a *minimum* storage duration and a per-request retrieval fee, so a 30-day archive you read every day costs more than you think.

Range requests let you read a byte range, which is how you do partial downloads, parallel multi-part downloads of one object, and efficient range scans over a Parquet or NDJSON dataset. Every serious analytics pipeline on object storage exploits this.

Replication is asynchronous and eventually consistent. Cross-region replication adds latency to the secondary, and a read from the secondary immediately after a write can miss it. Design for that, or accept a single region.

The rule of thumb: object storage is for bytes, not for rows. It has no index, no transaction, no partial update, and no cheap random write. It is excellent for the source of truth for large immutable files, cheap archival, and lakehouse landing zones, and it is the wrong place for a mutable 200-byte record.
commonMistakes: assuming a write is instantly searchable; from-based deep pagination; sorting on _score alone with a paginated request; aggregations on a text field; keyword without ignore_above thought; synonyms in a production index with no reindex plan; a non-deterministic sort; using must for filters; expecting COUNT(*) from a terms agg to be exact on a large index; claiming exactly-once; windowing on processing time; leaving incomplete multipart uploads alive forever; trusting a multipart ETag as an MD5; a presigned URL that lets the client choose the key.
practiceTasks: index 500k products with a deliberately dirty feed (missing fields, a field that is sometimes a number and sometimes a string, a field that is sometimes null) and watch dynamic mapping guess wrong; then set dynamic: strict and add templates, and index again. Build a query with a phrase filter, a filter-clause tenant predicate, a facet, and a function_score decay, and measure the difference between filters in must and in filter. Then implement search_after with a PIT and prove that pagination is stable while you keep indexing new documents. Finally, put a flattened field, a nested array of objects, and a keyword field in one mapping and write a query for each.

```go
        Bucket:      aws.String(bucket),

    }, s3.WithPresignExpires(ttl))

}
```

```typescript
// idempotent partial-batch handler: process items, report only the failures
import { SQSEvent, SQSBatchResponse, Handler } from "aws-lambda";

const process = async (id: string): Promise<void> => {
  await orders.markProcessed(id);   // idempotent: keyed by event id, conditional write
};

export const handler: Handler<SQSEvent, SQSBatchResponse> = async (event) => {
  const failures: { itemIdentifier: string }[] = [];
  await Promise.all(
    event.Records.map(async (r) => {
      try {
        const body = JSON.parse(r.body);
        await process(body.orderId);
      } catch (err) {
        console.error("order processing failed", { msg: r.messageId, err });
        failures.push({ itemIdentifier: r.messageId });   // only the failures retried
      }
    })
  );
  return { batchItemFailures: failures };
};
```

```python
import os, time, logging, json

COLD_THRESHOLD_MS = 500
_t0 = time.perf_counter()          # module import time == INIT proxy
logger = logging.getLogger()

def _cold() -> bool:
    # exec_env only exists when the platform provides it
    return bool(os.environ.get("AWS_EXECUTION_ENV"))

def handler(event, context):
    now = time.perf_counter()
    init_ms = (_t0 - START) * 1000  # module-level timestamp
    cold = _cold() and init_ms > COLD_THRESHOLD_MS
    logger.info(json.dumps({
        "event": "invocation",
        "function": context.function_name,
        "request_id": context.aws_request_id,
        "cold_start": cold,
        "init_ms": round(init_ms, 1),
        "duration_ms": round((now - START) * 1000, 1),
        "memory_mb": int(os.environ.get("AWS_LAMBDA_INITIALIZATION_TYPE", "0") or 0) or 512,
        "remaining_ms": context.get_remaining_time_in_millis(),
    }))
    return {"statusCode": 200, "body": json.dumps({"ok": True})}

START = time.perf_counter()
```

```go
// Server: issue a short-lived presigned PUT for a client-side direct upload
func presignPut(s3 *s3.Client, bucket, key, contentType string, ttl time.Duration) (string, error) {
    out, err := s3.PresignPutObject(context.Background(), &s3.PutObjectInput{
        Bucket:      aws.String(bucket),
        Key:         aws.String(key),
        ContentType: aws.String(contentType),
    }, s3.WithPresignExpires(ttl))
    return out.URL, err
}
```

```typescript
// idempotent partial-batch handler: process items, report only the failures
import { SQSEvent, SQSBatchResponse, Handler } from "aws-lambda";

const process = async (id: string): Promise<void> => {
  await orders.markProcessed(id);   // idempotent: keyed by event id, conditional write
};

export const handler: Handler<SQSEvent, SQSBatchResponse> = async (event) => {
  const failures: { itemIdentifier: string }[] = [];
  await Promise.all(
    event.Records.map(async (r) => {
      try {
        const body = JSON.parse(r.body);
        await process(body.orderId);
      } catch (err) {
        console.error("order processing failed", { msg: r.messageId, err });
        failures.push({ itemIdentifier: r.messageId });   // only the failures retried
      }
    })
  );
  return { batchItemFailures: failures };
};
```

```python
import os, time, logging, json

COLD_THRESHOLD_MS = 500
_t0 = time.perf_counter()          # module import time == INIT proxy
logger = logging.getLogger()

def _cold() -> bool:
    # exec_env only exists when the platform provides it
    return bool(os.environ.get("AWS_EXECUTION_ENV"))

def handler(event, context):
    now = time.perf_counter()
    init_ms = (_t0 - START) * 1000  # module-level timestamp
    cold = _cold() and init_ms > COLD_THRESHOLD_MS
    logger.info(json.dumps({
        "event": "invocation",
        "function": context.function_name,
        "request_id": context.aws_request_id,
        "cold_start": cold,
        "init_ms": round(init_ms, 1),
        "duration_ms": round((now - START) * 1000, 1),
        "memory_mb": int(os.environ.get("AWS_LAMBDA_INITIALIZATION_TYPE", "0") or 0) or 512,
        "remaining_ms": context.get_remaining_time_in_millis(),
    }))
    return {"statusCode": 200, "body": json.dumps({"ok": True})}

START = time.perf_counter()
```

```yaml
route:
```

topics.referenceMarkdown:
```
user journey:  browse → search → add to cart → checkout → pay → confirmation email

SLI (availability):  the proportion of *valid* requests that return a non-5xx response,
                     over 30 days, for the tier-1 journeys only.
SLI (latency):       the proportion of valid requests that complete within 300ms (p95),
                     over 30 days.
SLI (correctness):   the proportion of completed payments whose amount and currency
                     match the order (from business data, not from HTTP codes).
SLI (freshness):     the proportion of the last 24h of data made available in under 15m.
SLI (durability):    the proportion of written records retained for 90 days.
```

```
90%   → a hobby/internal tool
99%   → a tool users can work around
99.5% → an internal business system
99.9% → "3 nines": ~43 min/day of downtime allowed  (many mainstream SaaS products)
99.95%→ ~22 min/day
99.99%→ ~4 min/day  (expensive; needs strong redundancy, caching, and automation)
99.999%→ ~4 min/month (requires major architectural commitments, and even then providers
                    do not offer it as a whole-platform SLA)
```

```
budget remaining = (target failure time − actual failure time) / target failure time

policy:
  budget remaining > 50%  →  normal release cadence, feature work prioritised
  budget remaining 25–50% →  freeze non-essential changes, reliability work first,
                            tighten test coverage, review alert thresholds
  budget remaining < 25%  →  freeze all releases except fixes; daily reliability review;
                            exec-visible; consider a "reliability sprint"
  budget exhausted        →  postmortem-led plan, no new features until restored
```

```
error budget burn rate = (1 − SLI_measured) / (1 − SLO_target)

1×  = burning exactly the budget (steady state, sustainable-ish)
2×  = you will exhaust a 30-day budget in 15 days
10× = you will exhaust it in 3 days
100× = you will exhaust it in ~7 hours   ← page immediately
```

```promql
# SLI: successful / total over the 30d window, for tier-1 journeys only
- record: service:sli_availability:ratio_rate30d
  expr: |
    sum(rate(http_requests_total{
            service="checkout", route=~"/v1/(checkout|payments)",
            status!~"5..", code!~"4..", probe!="true"}[30d]))
    / sum(rate(http_requests_total{
            service="checkout", route=~"/v1/(checkout|payments)",
            code!~"4..", probe!="true"}[30d]))

# Allowed failure fraction
- record: service:slo_target:ratio
  expr: vector(0.999)

# Burn rate (how many times faster than sustainable)
- record: service:error_budget_burn:rate30d
  expr: |
    (1 - service:sli_availability:ratio_rate30d)
      / (1 - service:slo_target:ratio)

# Error budget remaining, as a fraction 0..1
- record: service:error_budget_remaining:ratio30d
  expr: |
```

```
1. Steady state    — define a measurable invariant (the "steady-state hypothesis")
2. Hypothesis      — "if X fails, our SLO degrades gracefully to Y and users in region
                     Z are unaffected"
3. Experiment design
     a. What fault     (pod kill, latency, packet loss, DNS failure, AZ loss, DB failover,
                        expired credential, disk full, CPU throttling, network partition)
     b. Blast radius  (one canary service, one AZ, 1% of traffic, staging first)
     c. Abort         (automatic: SLO burn > X for Y min → auto-abort; manual kill switch)
     d. Verify        (observability must be in place BEFORE the experiment)
4. Run it          — prefer production, with a small blast radius
5. Analyse         — did the system behave as hypothesised? What was surprising?
6. Fix and re-run  — the experiment becomes a permanent test once it passes
```

```
Experiment: "Database failover does not cause duplicate order creation"

Steady-state hypothesis:
  During a DB failover, the checkout error rate stays below 1% for the 2 minutes of the
  failover, no order is created twice (checked by order count vs. payment count), and
  the service becomes ready within 90s.

Blast radius:
  Multi-AZ RDS failover for the checkout database. Announced in #eng. Stakeholders: DB
  owner, payments owner. Window: Tuesday 14:00 UTC. Abort condition: error rate > 5% for
  60s, or any detected duplicate order.

Procedure:
  1. Confirm dashboards + alerts are live and the SLO alert is not silenced.
  2. `aws rds failover-db-cluster --db-cluster-identifier checkout --force-failover`
  3. Watch: SLI (availability ratio), latency histogram, order/payment count diff,
     readiness failures, connection pool saturation.
  4. Record MTTR to steady state.

Result:
  - Availability dropped to 98.9% for 94s (within the 1% hypothesis, barely).
  - MTTR to steady state: 94s.
  - No duplicate orders (idempotency key check passed).
  - SURPRISE: 2,300 HTTP 500s with "connection reset" in the first 8 seconds because
    the connection pool had no retry-on-connect-reset, and RDS Proxy (new) took 40s to
    re-establish pools.
Action items:
  1. Configure the pooler with `connection_init_query` validation and a smaller
     recycle window (owner: dba, due 2 weeks).
  2. Add a retry-with-jitter only on ECONNRESET during a known failover window
     (owner: checkout, due 3 weeks).
  3. Re-run this experiment after the fixes, scheduled monthly.
```

```
DB failover      → error rate < 1%, no duplicate writes, recovery < 2 min
AZ loss          → no loss of quorum, capacity sufficient at 2× load, no data loss
One pod killed   → zero 5xx (ALB drains), recovery < 30s, no restart storm
Secret rotated   → no mass restart, no extended 401s
Latency +500ms   → p99 within 2× SLO, no retry amplification (error rate stable)
Disk full        → writes fail loudly, reads served, no silent corruption
Duplicate msgs   → zero duplicate side effects
Expired TLS cert → explicit error, not a silent downgrade; renewals actually run
```

```markdown
# Runbook: CheckoutErrorBudgetBurnFast

## What this means
Checkout is failing more than 14.4× faster than our 99.9% SLO allows. Users are
seeing errors right now.

## Dashboard
https://grafana.internal/d/checkout-overview?from=now-1h   (panels: "Are users
seeing errors?", "Is latency breaching the SLO?")

## Confirm (2 minutes)
1. `curl -s localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode \
    'query=service:sli_availability:ratio_rate5m{service="checkout"}'`
   → if the ratio is back above the threshold, this was a spike; watch for 10 min.
2. Check the deploy markers on the dashboard: was there a release in the last hour?
3. Check which route: `service:http_errors:ratio_rate5m{service="checkout"}` by route.

## Mitigate (in this order)
1. **Roll back the last checkout deploy** (usually the cause):
   `deployctl rollback --service checkout --to-previous` (2–5 min, no code needed).
2. **Kill the feature flag** if the dashboard shows the failure is confined to
   `/v1/checkout`: `flags set checkout.new_pricing=false` (instant).
3. **Scale out**: `deployctl scale --service checkout --count 20`. NOTE: this does NOT
   help if the cause is a per-instance circuit breaker or a downstream rate limit.
4. **Drain the queue** if `OrdersQueueAge > 300s`: scale the consumer, do not purge.

## Diagnose (only if the mitigation above did not restore the SLO)
1. `loki` query: `{app="checkout"} |= "error"` over the incident window.
2. Jump from the p99 exemplar to the trace (Grafana: click the histogram bucket).
3. Check dependency health: `deployctl status --service payments`, PSP status page.
4. Read `docs/architecture/checkout.md` — the PSP timeout/breaker configuration.

## Escalate
- >15 min without mitigation → escalate to secondary, then manager.
- Any data-integrity signal → declare SEV1, notify security/comms.
- Suspected security issue → do not debug in prod; page security, preserve evidence.

## Post-incident
Update the alert if it was noisy; add a runbook gap to the incident doc.
```

```
1. Measure toil: log every on-call task for two weeks; classify as
   P0 (mitigation during incidents) vs R (routine).
2. Attack the top 3 by hours per month.
3. Automate: IaC instead of console; scripts instead of copy-paste; auto-remediation
   for known failure modes (restart on crash-loop, scale on queue age, auto-rollback
   on SLO burn).
4. Delete the alert if the toil is caused by noise.
5. Re-measure. Target: on-call time < 10% of engineering time; > 25% means the
   service is not supportable as designed and needs an investment proposal.
```

topics.referenceMarkdown:
```
user journey:  browse → search → add to cart → checkout → pay → confirmation email

SLI (availability):  the proportion of *valid* requests that return a non-5xx response,
                     over 30 days, for the tier-1 journeys only.
SLI (latency):       the proportion of valid requests that complete within 300ms (p95),
                     over 30 days.
SLI (correctness):   the proportion of completed payments whose amount and currency
                     match the order (from business data, not from HTTP codes).
SLI (freshness):     the proportion of the last 24h of data made available in under 15m.
SLI (durability):    the proportion of written records retained for 90 days.
```

```
90%   → a hobby/internal tool
99%   → a tool users can work around
99.5% → an internal business system
99.9% → "3 nines": ~43 min/day of downtime allowed  (many mainstream SaaS products)
99.95%→ ~22 min/day
99.99%→ ~4 min/day  (expensive; needs strong redundancy, caching, and automation)
99.999%→ ~4 min/month (requires major architectural commitments, and even then providers
                    do not offer it as a whole-platform SLA)
```

```
budget remaining = (target failure time − actual failure time) / target failure time

policy:
  budget remaining > 50%  →  normal release cadence, feature work prioritised
  budget remaining 25–50% →  freeze non-essential changes, reliability work first,
                            tighten test coverage, review alert thresholds
  budget remaining < 25%  →  freeze all releases except fixes; daily reliability review;
                            exec-visible; consider a "reliability sprint"
  budget exhausted        →  postmortem-led plan, no new features until restored
```

```
error budget burn rate = (1 − SLI_measured) / (1 − SLO_target)

1×  = burning exactly the budget (steady state, sustainable-ish)
2×  = you will exhaust a 30-day budget in 15 days
10× = you will exhaust it in 3 days
100× = you will exhaust it in ~7 hours   ← page immediately
```

```markdown
# INC-2026-03-04: Checkout returning 500s for ~18% of requests

Severity:   SEV1 (user-visible payment failure; no workaround)
Started:    2026-03-04 09:12 UTC
Mitigated:  2026-03-04 09:41 UTC (29 min)
Resolved:   2026-03-04 10:05 UTC (53 min total)
Commander:  rprem      Scribe: jdoe      Comms: ksmith
Status page: https://status.example.com/incidents/2026-03-04-checkout-500s

## Impact
~18% of checkout attempts returned HTTP 500 between 09:12 and 09:41 UTC.
Estimated affected users: ~4,100 (18% of 22,800 checkouts in the window).
No successful orders were lost; orders that reached `payment.authorized` completed.
No data corruption identified.

## Detection
Prometheus multi-window SLO alert `CheckoutErrorBudgetBurnFast` fired at 09:13:41
(1m41s after onset). Two customer support tickets arrived at 09:14 (ahead of the alert).

## Timeline (all UTC)
09:12:03  Deployment `checkout@v2.31.0` completed (10.6k–10.8k, autoscaled 4→8 tasks).
09:13:41  SLO burn alert fired (14.4× over 1h and 5m windows). Routed to #checkout-oncall.
09:14:20  IC (rprem) declared SEV1; channel #inc-2026-03-04-checkout-500s opened.
09:16:05  Scribe started this document.
09:17:30  IC hypothesis: "the 09:12 deploy" — p99 rose and 500s started within 60s.
09:18:10  Tech lead traced 500s to `payments/authorize`: `GatewayTimeout` returned when
          the PSP response took >3s. New deploy added a 2s per-attempt timeout with
          retries; 3 retries × 3s = 9s > the ALB idle timeout (60s) is irrelevant, but
          the PSP's own circuit breaker (5 failures) opened, so all subsequent calls
          failed fast for 19 minutes.
09:21:00  Mitigation attempted: scaled tasks 8→20. No effect (the PSP circuit breaker
          is per-instance state, and the breaker is closed only by a cooldown timer).
09:26:15  Decision: roll back. Rationale: the only recent change; 15 min of debugging
          has not identified a safe forward fix.
09:28:40  Rollback of `checkout@v2.31.0` initiated via the deployment pipeline.
09:33:10  Rollback complete on all tasks; circuit breakers recovered after cooldown.
09:41:00  Error rate back to 0.02% (baseline). Mitigation declared at 09:41.
10:05:00  30 min of stable p99 (<200ms) and error rate. Incident resolved.
09:20     Status page updated: "Identified".
09:35     Status page updated: "Monitoring".

## Contributing factors (short version; full analysis in the postmortem)
1. Timeout + retry change multiplied the worst-case request duration beyond the PSP's
   breaker threshold without a circuit breaker.
2. No synthetic payment-path check in staging with a slow PSP.
3. The SLO alert took 1m41s to detect; a synthetic probe would have caught it in ~30s.
4. Scaling did not help, but we spent 5 minutes on it — no runbook entry for "PSP
   breaker is per-instance".

## What went well
- SLO alert worked and routed correctly.
- Rollback was available and took 5 minutes.
- Comms were ahead of the customer-reported impact.

## Follow-ups (tracked in INC-2026-03-04 action items)
1. Circuit breaker on all outbound PSP calls (owner: jdoe, due 2026-03-18)
2. Per-attempt timeout must be < (total budget − ALB idle timeout); add a unit test

3. Synthetic checkout with an injected 3s PSP latency in staging (owner: ksmith, due 2026-03-25)
4. Runbook: "PSP timeouts" including "scaling does not help" (owner: jdoe, due 2026-03-15)
```

```
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter:

delay(n) = min(cap, base × 2^n) × random(0.5 .. 1.5)

attempt 0: immediate
attempt 1: ~100ms   ±50%
attempt 2: ~200ms   ±50%
attempt 3: ~400ms   ±50%   (cap 2s)
total worst case ≈ base×(2^n−1) + cap, and MUST be < the caller's own timeout
```

```python
import random, itertools, functools

class TransientError(Exception): ...
class PermanentError(Exception): ...

def retryable(fn, *, attempts=3, base=0.1, cap=2.0, deadline_budget=5.0,
              retry_on=(TransientError, TimeoutError)):
    """Exponential backoff with full jitter, bounded by a total time budget."""
    end = time.monotonic() + deadline_budget
    last = None
    for i in range(attempts):
        try:
            return fn()
        except retry_on as e:
            last = e
            if i == attempts - 1: break
            delay = min(cap, base * (2 ** i))
            jitter = random.uniform(0.5, 1.5) * delay        # full jitter
            remaining = end - time.monotonic()
            if remaining <= jitter: break                     # no time left: give up
            time.sleep(min(jitter, remaining))
    raise last

# Usage with an idempotency key so retries cannot double-charge
def charge(order, key: str):
    return retryable(lambda: psp.charge(order, idempotency_key=key),
                     retry_on=(TransientError,), attempts=3, deadline_budget=4.0)
```

```go
// Go: the context deadline is the retry budget; never retry past it
func (c *Client) Get(ctx context.Context, key string) (*Item, error) {
    backoff := backoff.NewExponentialBackOff(backoff.WithMaxElapsedTime(3 * time.Second))
    var lastErr error
    op := func() error {
        req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, c.base+key, nil)
        resp, err := c.http.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return transient(err) }                    // network-level
        defer resp.Body.Close()
        switch {
        case resp.StatusCode >= 500 || resp.StatusCode == 429:
            lastErr = fmt.Errorf("upstream %d", resp.StatusCode)
            return lastErr                                          // retryable
        case resp.StatusCode >= 400:
            return permanent(fmt.Errorf("upstream %d", resp.StatusCode)) // stop
        default:
            return decode(resp)
        }
    }
    err := backoff.Retry(op, backoff.WithContext(op, ctx))
    return nil, err   // ctx deadline bounds everything
}
```

```java
record SearchExecutor(SearchClient c, ExecutorService exec) {
  Result search(Query q) throws RejectedExecutionException {
    var f = exec.submit(() -> c.query(q));
```

```
Chain A (retry storm):
PSP slow → checkout timeouts → retries at gateway AND service → 3×3 load on a
already-struggling PSP → PSP total outage → circuit breaker finally opens →
checkout 500s → but PSP never recovers because it is being hammered by the tail.

Chain B (timeout cascade):
DB slows (missing index after a release) → checkout read timeout 30s → every request
holds a DB connection for 30s → pool of 20 exhausted → queue builds → memory grows →
GC pauses → all requests slow → load balancer timeouts at 60s → users see 504s.

Chain C (bulkhead absent):
One slow optional dependency (recommendations) with a 10s timeout → all 200 threads
blocked on it → core checkout requests cannot get a thread → total outage of a feature
that is supposed to be optional.

Chain D (hedging without cancellation):
p99 spikes → hedging doubles load → p99 spikes more → more hedging → positive feedback
loop → self-inflicted outage. Fix: hedge factor > 1, abort the loser, and only for reads.
```
